docs.title: CoreWeave debt selloff poses limited risk to global banks, J.P. Morgan says
docs.text:
By Siddarth S
- Most global banks have limited exposure to CoreWeave , J.P. Morgan estimated on Tuesday, after the Nvidia-backed cloud company 's stocks and bonds slumped last week on investor worries over debt financing .
 AI infrastructure spending has been rattling investors globally as tech companies are on a fundraising spree from private-credit investors, banks and bond markets to rapidly expand, while questions over returns on these investments swell.
 While large US investment banks along with Japan's MUFG could potentially have exposure of about $1 billion to $3 billion in CoreWeave, most European and Asian players have less than $500 million, the Wall Street brokerage said.
 Advt 
Much of this is through delayed draw term loans, J.P. Morgan said, which are largely held through special-purpose vehicles, with capital released as projects meet milestones.
 "From the perspective of financing banks, we view bank exposures to CoreWeave as well managed and very well secured," J.P. Morgan analysts led by Kian Abouhossein said in a note.
The brokerage said estimates are based on "simplified assumptions" because banks provide limited disclosure on their exposure to the AI investment cycle.
J.P. Morgan has an "overweight" rating on CoreWeave with a target price of $125 for 2027-end.
 The cloud company has about $24 billion of committed delayed draw term loans, including $15 billion drawn and $9 billion undrawn, according to the brokerage.
CoreWeave, which provides high-performance computing infrastructure for AI, has secured tens of billions of dollars in contracts with major technology companies. The company has about $50 billion in debt.
 Last week, the yield on CoreWeave's notes due 2031 touched almost 16%, while the cost of insuring against the company's debt rose to around 1,000 basis points.
The key risk facing banks is a mismatch between upfront spending on AI infrastructure and revenue received over time, J.P. Morgan said, adding that it expects CoreWeave's free cash flow to remain negative until 2030.
 (Reporting by Siddarth S in Bengaluru; Editing by Harikrishnan Nair)

docs.title: French bond yields near 24-year high as new protests loom
docs.text:
France's government bond yields climbed further on Tuesday after their biggest daily rise in nearly a month, with investors remaining cautious as protest groups announced a new round of demonstrations planned for Saturday.
 French bond prices, which move inversely to yields, slid on Monday after weekend protests led to riots across France, adding to the difficulties the government faces in reducing its large deficit.

France's OAT yields were up 3 basis points (bps) at 4.96%; it reached 4.9937%, its highest since July 2002, in early October. The yield gap between OATs and Bunds widened by 5.5 bps to 152.50 bps. It reached 158.67 basis points in early October, the highest level since November 2011.
The Italian spread also rose 4.5 bps to 113.51 bps.
"While not pivotal to the overall process, today's vote on the revenue side of the (French) budget bill takes on a little more importance as a near-term signal," Jamie Searle, European rate strategist at Citi, said.
 Live Events
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen and hard-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon extended their lead over other candidates in a poll published last week - before the weekend's events, a scenario analysts view as the least favourable for efforts to reduce France's fiscal deficit.
"The protests highlight that any government will struggle to implement the required reforms and savings against broader public resistance," Benjamin Schroeder, senior rates strategist at ING, said.
"The beneficiaries (of the protests' political fallout) appear to be the right and centre candidates, while on the far left, Melenchon's chances of winning the presidential race have been pared back," he added, arguing that Melenchon's plans are viewed as among the most controversial.
Meanwhile, euro zone benchmark Bund yields edged lower but traded within their recent range after last week's drop, as persistent energy price pressures kept investors from scaling back bets on further European Central Bank rate hikes .
Oil prices advanced on Tuesday, with Brent hovering around a five-month high.
Analysts said it will be difficult to materially reduce the market's bias towards further rate hikes, as a credible decline in energy prices remains elusive and winter weather is likely to play a crucial role in determining the path of gas prices.
Germany's 10-year government bond yields, the euro zone benchmark, were down 2 bps to 3.43%. They have moved between about 3.40% and 3.50% since early this month, barring last Thursday's drop, when tech stocks took a beating.
Germany's 2-year government bond yield, more sensitive to policy rate expectations, fell 1.5 bps to 3.07%.

As preparations for the Union Budget 2026–27 gather pace, the groundwork underway signals a clear policy intent to accelerate domestic demand, revive private investment and generate employment, according to a budget note by Motilal Oswal Financial Services (MOFSL). The brokerage has identified five stocks across auto, agriculture, defence, financials and infrastructure themes, which it believes could deliver strong gains for investors.
 "The Budget is expected to focus on income-tax, GST, and customs simplification to enhance ease of doing business and support fiscal consolidation, alongside targeted support for agriculture, MSMEs, manufacturing, infrastructure, higher defence capex, EVs, and renewables through credit and incentives," the note authored by Research Analysts Sneha Poddar and Rekha Jaat said.
A strong capital expenditure thrust across highways, logistics, defence, rail freight corridors and connectivity is anticipated, complemented by emphasis on skilling, rural prosperity, women empowerment, AI adoption, climate action and digital finance to anchor India’s next phase of economic expansion, the note added.
The finance ministry started work on the Union Budget for 2026-27 from October 9 as per a circular issued by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA).
The preparations come against the backdrop of an additional 50% US tariff on most Indian goods and other external headwinds. These have raised risks to India's growth and jobs outlook, prompting calls for stronger support to the export sector.
 Live Events
 5 stocks to buy: 
The stocks recommended by MOFSL are TVS Motor Company, UPL , Bharat Dynamics (BDL), M&M Financial Services and Dalmia Bharat , and each of these stocks has been assigned a 20% weight.
 1) TVS Motors: TVS Motors continues to outperform peers and is well-positioned to benefit from the budget’s push to boost domestic consumption and rural demand through higher allocations, income support, and infrastructure spending.
MOFSL said that improving rural sentiment, strong entry-level recovery and sustained two-wheeler demand will be key triggers. Moreover, the company's market share gains, easing discounts, and margin expansion will provide strong earnings visibility. The Apache and Ntorq maker remains its top pick in OEMs.
 2) UPL: The diversified agrochemical leader is well positioned to benefit from the union budget push riding on rural prosperity via higher agri credit, MSME support, and value-chain strengthening, lifting farmer incomes and crop-protection demand.
The company's strong points are stronger volumes, export tailwinds, improved working-capital discipline and post-bond-repayment balance-sheet strength, the brokerage note said. The company's rising focus on speciality chemicals supports solid 2HFY26 growth.
 3) Bharat Dynamics: Bharat Dynamics (BDL), a defence play, has a robust Rs 50,000 crore order pipeline over five years, with Rs 20,000 crore targeted in 2-3 years. This aligns with the expected defence capex surge and infra push.
The recent Rs 2.5 lakh crore DAC approvals for missiles, undersea warfare, and naval arms leverage BDL's tactical/strategic expertise, propelling FY31 turnover to Rs 100bn via indigenisation and lower provisions, the note said.
 4) M&M Financial Services: M&M Financial is poised for Union Budget 2026-27 benefits via rural prosperity, MSME credit, and employment focus, driving PV/tractor loan growth amid surging volumes from festive demand, GST cuts, and restocking.
The company targets Rs 3 lakh crore in assets under management (AUM) by 2030, which is at an 18-20% CAGR, bolstered by AI underwriting, lower credit costs, controlled opex, and margin stability for strong earnings visibility in retail portfolios.
 5) Dalmia Bharat: The cement company benefits from the budget’s infra capex surge, PMAY rural housing, and urban projects, driving cement volume growth.
Dalmia Bharat is a low-cost cement producer with high blending ratios, green power and low freight. The company is targeting 62 mtpa capacity by FY28, and its cost optimisation endeavours will likely lift EBITDA margins amid sector consolidation.

Reliance Power 's board of directors on Monday approved the issuance of up to 46.20 crore equity shares/warrants worth Rs 1,525 crore via preferential allotment mode.
 The board has set the issue price at Rs 33 per share.
The issue price of equity shares/warrants is at a discount of 13% over Monday's closing price of Rs 38.15 on the NSE. The announcement was made after market hours and Reliance Power shares on Monday ended with gains of Rs 1.81 or 4.98% over the previous closing price.
 Reliance Infrastructure Limited, the promoter of the company, will enhance its equity stake by over Rs 600 crore, a company filing said. The other investors in the preferential issue are Authum Investment and Infrastructure Limited and Sanatan Financial Advisory Services Private Limited.
The proceeds from the preferential issue will be utilised to expand business operations directly and/or through investment in subsidiaries and joint ventures, debt reduction and for general corporate purposes, the filing said.

The markets worldwide are waiting with bated breath on what will be a historic policy announcement from the US Federal Reserve , where the central bank is expected to usher in a rate cut cycle.
 The announcement will be made at 11:30 pm IST (Indian Standard Time) on Wednesday.
If analysts are to be believed, the US Fed is all but certain to cut interest rates for the first time in more than four years.
However, there is no consensus on the quantum of reduction. Some are predicting a smaller cut of a quarter of a percentage point, while others believe a bigger half-point reduction is in the works.
Senior officials at the US central bank, including Powell, have indicated that a rate cut is coming, as inflation eases toward the bank's long-term target of 2%, and the labour market continues to cool in the post-Covid economy.
 Live Events
If the Fed starts the rate cut cycle, the Reserve Bank of India is also expected to follow suit.
A smaller cut would be a more predictable move, while a bigger cut would do more to boost demand — while also running the risk of reigniting inflation.
 WATCH LIVE TODAY: Press conference with #FOMC Chair Powell at 2:30 p.m. ET: https://t.co/1uJrua5qsH https://t.co/FJa6TbkDMt pic.twitter.com/87g5NJITsz 
— Federal Reserve (@federalreserve) September 18, 2024 
By the end 2024, markets are expecting a total reduction of at least 100 basis points in the first rate cut cycle in over 4 years since 2020.
But whether the Fed goes for 25 or 50 bps, the biggest trigger for stock prices to move up or down would be Powell's motivation behind the cut.
Asset classes from stocks, currencies and fixed income could all log swings in the immediate aftermath of the Fed decision.
While easing US interest rates are directionally positive for equities in general, “we should keep in mind interest rates are just one variable in a complex adaptive system that determines the direction of Indian equity markets”, said Anoop Vijaykumar, Investments and Head of Research at Capitalmind.

docs.title: Top stocks to buy for short term: Just Dial, BSE, Orient Hotels - Target price, stop-loss by Anand Rathi's expert
docs.text:
Top stocks to buy for short term: Stock market benchmark Nifty 50 ended with a strong loss of 257 points, or 1.11%, at 22,888.95 on Monday, 19 October, snapping its two-day winning run, due to persistent global and domestic macroeconomic concernsHigher brent crude prices amid geopolitical tensions and supply-side uncertainties have fuelled concerns over inflation flare-up. Besides, foreign capital outflow, elevated bond yields in the US and chances of further rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve are also key concerns, keeping market sentiment low.Jigar S. Patel, Senior Manager of Equity Technical Research at Anand Rathi Share and Stock Brokers, underscored that from its 8 October low of 22,180, the Nifty has seen some decent rise, which reinforces the view of avoiding panic selling during the breakdown near 22,200."We maintain our 'buy on dips' stance. The immediate support zone is placed at 22,800–22,600, with 22,600 emerging as a crucial level to defend. On the upside, 23,200 remains the immediate resistance. A sustained breakout above this level could open the door towards 23,600 in the coming week," said Patel.For Bank Nifty, Patel said that a sustained move above 56,000 could trigger further upside towards 57,000, which remains a crucial resistance level. On the downside, support has shifted higher to the 55,200–54,700 zone, making it an important area to monitor."As long as the index sustains above this support band, the near-term outlook remains positive. A decisive breakout above 56,000 would further strengthen bullish momentum and improve the prospects of an advance towards 57,000," said Patel.Stock picks for short termJust Dial | Previous close: ₹731.75 | Target price: ₹800 | Stop-loss: ₹670Just Dial is showing encouraging technical signals, with the stock witnessing a breakout after a period of consolidation just above its 50, 100 and 200-day exponential moving averages (DEMAs).This consolidation indicates price stability and improving buying interest, while the subsequent breakout suggests a potential continuation of the upward momentum.The technical outlook is further supported by the Relative Strength Index (RSI) on both the daily and weekly charts trading above 60, indicating strong momentum across short-term and medium-term timeframes."Sustained trading above these key moving averages could strengthen the bullish structure and support further upside. Traders may consider buying the stock for a potential target of ₹800, while maintaining a strict stop-loss at ₹670 to manage downside risk," said Patel.Oriental Hotels | Previous close: ₹148.99 | Target price: ₹171 | Stop-loss: ₹140Orient Hotels is displaying encouraging technical signals, with the stock witnessing a strong breakout following a period of consolidation just above its 50-day DEMA.This consolidation indicates price stability and the formation of a potential support base, while the subsequent breakout suggests improving buying interest and the possibility of further upside.The bullish outlook is supported by the Relative Strength Index (RSI) on both the daily and weekly charts, which is around or above the 60 mark, indicating strengthening momentum across short-term and medium-term timeframes.
"Sustained trading above the 50-day DEMA could help maintain the positive price structure. Traders may consider buying the stock with a target of ₹171, while maintaining a strict stop-loss at ₹140 to manage downside risk," said Patel.
BSE | Previous close: ₹3,336 | Buy between ₹3,400– ₹3,250 | Target price: ₹4,000 | Stop-loss: ₹3,000
BSE is displaying encouraging technical signals, with a hidden bullish divergence emerging on the weekly chart, indicating the potential continuation of its prevailing uptrend.
This pattern typically forms when the price records a higher low while the Relative Strength Index (RSI) forms a lower low, suggesting that the underlying bullish trend may remain intact despite intermittent corrections.
The weekly RSI near the 40 level adds to the positive outlook, as this zone has historically acted as a support cushion during healthy uptrends.Additionally, the 50-week Exponential Moving Average (EMA) coincides with the previous breakout zone, creating a confluence of technical support."This alignment strengthens the overall setup and improves the risk-reward proposition. Investors may consider accumulating the stock in the ₹3,400– ₹3,250 range, with an upside target of ₹4,000. A strict stop-loss at ₹3,000 should be maintained on a closing basis," said Patel.Read all market-related news hereDisclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. The views and recommendations expressed are those of the expert, not Mint. docs.title: Dussehra 2026 special: Top 3 stocks to buy; ICICI Bank, Adani Ports, Reliance Industries | Target price by Mahesh M Ojha
docs.text:
They used to celebrate crop harvests and adopted a gifting culture, handing over crops and domesticated animals to their near and dear ones. So, in India, investment existed even when there was no financial instrument like currency. Buying of land and domestic animals through the payment of money, called ‘Pana’ is available during the Vedic Period. Later on, the investment shifted towards precious metals like gold and silver, as well as their ornaments, and this trend continues. In modern India, people with abundant wealth have the luxury to invest in physical gold, silver, land, etc. However, for a marginal retail investor, physical gold and silver have shifted to electronic and digital gold and silver. In digital gold and silver, an investor can invest with a Re 1 investment. Likewise, if an investor can't afford to buy land paying a hefty amount upfront, they can buy a unit of Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs). Similarly, on an auspicious occasion, there is a tradition in India to start a new company or its subsidiary, or announce a new company for the next generation. However, this is not a piece of cake for every individual. For such marginal investors, there are listed companies whose shares are available for buying and selling on the BSE and the NSE. A retail investor can buy stocks of companies listed on the BSE and the NSE, and these stocks are expected to grow over time. For stock investors planning to add some value picks to their portfolios this Dussehra, Mahesh M Ojha, VP — Research and Business Development at KC Securities, has recommended three long-term shares, predicting a whopping return by next year's Dussehra. Those three shares are ICICI Bank, Adani Ports, and Reliance Industries. Predicting a turnaround on Dalal Street in the near-term, Mahesh M Ojha of KC Securities said, “The average P/E of Nifty 50 and Sensex is fairly priced at around 19.50, well below the last 5 years and last 10 years median price. The Bank Nifty index is also trading at an average P/E multiple of 13.25, which can be considered fairly valued, as the last 2-5 years' average P/E range for the Bank Nifty is 12.50 to 16.70.” Ojha said that large-caps can be a good bet for long-term investors planning to start a new investment in Dussehra 2026 and recommended buying ICICI Bank, Adani Ports, and Reliance Industries shares for a one-year time horizon. Regarding special stock recommendations on Dussehra 2026, Mahesh Ojha of KC Securities unveiled this strategy while investing in his value picks: 1] ICICI Bank: Buy in the range of 1,360 to ₹ 1,380 | Target price ₹ 1,650; 2]Adani Ports: Buy in the range of ₹ 1,740 to ₹ 1,765 | Target price ₹ 2,050; and 3] Reliance Industries: Buy in the range of ₹ 1,195 to ₹ 1,202 | Target price ₹ 1500+. Disclaimer: This story is for educational and informational purposes only. The views and recommendations above are those of individual analysts or broking companies, not Mint. We advise investors to check with certified financial experts before making any investment decisions. Asit Manohar has nearly two decades of experience in the mainstream media. In this period, he has served esteemed media organisations like NDTV Profit, The Economic Times, and Zee Business. He has been working at LiveMint Digital since April 2021. During these two decades of journey in mainstream media, Asit has mainly covered external affairs, markets and personal finance. However, his earliest beats include railways, SME, MSME, and politics (Congress beat). Some of his features on political, economic, and foreign policy are documented in the parliamentary records.

While pursuing his MA (Mass Communication, Session 2004-06), Asit began his media career as a stringer at All India Radio in Varanasi. At AIR Varanasi, Asit worked with the Gyanvani, Yuvvani and Vividh Bharti teams. After working for nearly one year at AIR Varanasi, he shifted to print journalism and started working as a stringer for the HT Media Ltd, Varanasi. At HT Media Ltd in Varanasi, he covered the BHU beat.

Asit has also worked with some brokerage houses. He has worked with Religare Broking and India Infoline, where he assisted the research team in developing and executing trade strategies for intraday cash, F&O, and commodities.

Asit is a Gold Medalist in MA (Mass Communication) from BHU, Varanasi. He did his BSc. (Hons) in Mathematics from Magadh University, Bodh Gaya.  Health ministry, Pharmacy Council of India differ over pharmacist service rules
 Priyanka Sharma 6 min read 20 Oct 2026, 02:31 PM IST 
 Summary
 The health ministry has declared the rules invalid, saying they were issued without government approval, according to two government officials and a circular reviewed by Mint. The PCI, however, maintains that it acted within its statutory powers.

 New Delhi: An unprecedented row has erupted between the Union health ministry and the Pharmacy Council of India (PCI), a statutory body under the ministry, over recently notified regulations governing the recruitment, promotion and service conditions of government pharmacists.
 The ministry has declared the rules invalid, according to a circular dated 12 October, saying they were issued without government approval, according to two government officials. Mint has reviewed the circular.
 The PCI, which had published the regulations in the Gazette of India on 10 June “with the approval of the Central Government”, maintains that it acted within its statutory powers.
 The Pharmacist Recruitment, Promotion and Service Regulations, 2025, issued by the PCI, seeks to establish an independent cadre of government pharmacists, their recruitment, promotions, service conditions and responsibilities.
 The health and family welfare ministry has emphasized that no such approval was ever granted and concluded that the regulations were ultra vires the Pharmacy Act, 1948, and beyond the legal powers of the PCI, rendering them non est (non-existent) in the eye of law, according to the government circular.
 Ultra vires , with roots in Latin, refers to actions that exceeded legal authority.
 Ultra vires, says ministry
 “The preamble to the said PCI notification claims that the Regulations were framed ‘with the approval of the Central Government,’” the 12 October circular read.
 “These regulations have been issued without the approval of the Central government, and as opined by Department of Legal Affairs (DoLA), the impugned regulations are ultra vires the Act and beyond the authority of the PCI and are therefore non est in the eye of law.” Non est , again from Latin, means “does not exist.”
 The ministry has directed the health secretaries of all states and Union territories, hospital divisions, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) and the Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) to take note of the order. Further, recruiting authorities and government healthcare departments have been instructed not to initiate or consider any administrative or regulatory action based on the invalid framework, the circular noted.
 Authorities in the loop: PCI
 The PCI contends that the health ministry was informed about the new regulations.
 “The Council has acted strictly within its statutory powers under the Pharmacy Act to safeguard public health and reform the profession. While qualifications have evolved over the years to BPharm, MPharm and PharmD, government pharmacists were still stuck with decades-old pay scales and structures. We formulated these recruitment and promotion regulations to address these legitimate demands,” PCI president Montu Patel told Mint on the phone.
 Addressing the ministry’s claim that the gazette notification was unapproved, Patel said, “Authorities were kept fully informed. We repeatedly sought their permissions but received neither an affirmative nor a negative reply. We eventually wrote to them stating that in the interest of the profession, we would proceed to notify the regulations, which we did with their complete knowledge. We have documented proof of every communication and will present all records.”
 The PCI regulates pharmacy education, training and professional practice in India under the Pharmacy Act, 1948, and oversees the registration of pharmacists.
 The ministry in response to Mint’ s queries pointed out that the PCI “is entrusted with regulating standards of pharmacy education.” "It is important to distinguish between regulation of pharmacy education and matters relating to recruitment, promotion, pay scales and cadre restructuring, which are governed by the applicable rules and procedures of the respective Central and State Government employing authorities,” it further added.
 Data from the PCI and the Central Bureau of Health Intelligence’s National Health Profile show that India has more than 1.6 million registered pharmacists, of whom around 400,000 work in the government sector. The rest are employed across retail pharmacies, healthcare facilities and the pharmaceutical industry.
 “In exercise of the powers conferred by section 10 and 18 of the Pharmacy Act, 1948, the Pharmacy Council of India, with the approval of the Central Government, hereby makes the regulations namely: Pharmacist Recruitment, Promotion and Service Regulations, 2025,” the 10 June notification said.
 Progressive rules, says lobby
 A pharmacist industry group asked the government to reconsider its stance and approve the framework proposed by the PCI. “The Pharmacy Council of India’s move to frame updated recruitment rules was an encouraging step taken strictly in the interest of pharmacists and pharmacy students. The government should have approved these regulations instead of stalling them,” said Shashi Bhushan Singh, president, Akhil Bhartiya Pharmacists Association.
 Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state with some 250 million people, has just around 7,700 pharmacist positions across community and primary health centres, Singh added, stressing the need for structured recruitment rules keeping safety in public health in mind.

docs.title: Why have fresh investments into gold FoFs been halted, and what should you do?
docs.text:
Mint Money Why have fresh investments into gold FoFs been halted, and what should you do? Ann Jacob 3 min read 20 Oct 2026, 10:26 AM IST Summary Restricting FoF inflows serves to limit foreign exchange leakage. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now About 20 mutual fund houses have reportedly halted fresh lump-sum investments, new SIPs (systematic investment plans) and top-ups in gold fund of funds (FoFs) following regulatory directives on 15 and 16 October. The step, as explained by experts, is designed to curb domestic gold import demand and relieve pressure on the rupee during the festive season, without disrupting direct ETF (exchange traded fund) investments. What changes? The fund houses of State Bank of India, Kotak Mahindra, ICICI Prudential, HDFC, Tata and DSP, along with others, have restricted new incremental flows into gold FoFs, though existing active SIPs will continue. “Fund houses have taken action only in gold fund of funds, not in gold ETFs ,” clarified Anil Ghelani, head of passive investments at DSP Mutual Fund. He emphasized that this is not a market-driven liquidity issue, unlike what was previously seen in micro-cap or small-cap funds, where massive inflows into relatively less liquid stocks created real risks during redemption in the category, while gold remained fully liquid. Also, the restriction targets only one specific entry route. “Today, if you want to buy any gold ETF, it is listed and actively traded on the NSE and BSE. You can go there and buy at any point in time,” Ghelani added. A gold FoF acts as a feeder pipe that invests in underlying gold ETFs. At DSP Mutual Fund, the gold FoF has ₹ 500 crore-600 crore of assets under management, representing roughly 20% of the ₹ 3,000 crore gold ETF total size. According to data from DSP MF, the total industry size of gold FoF stood at ₹ 47,359 crore as of August compared with ₹ 53,638 crore in March and ₹ 22,837 crore in September 2025. Ghelani added that this is a structural posturing and investors need not panic by considering these restrictions as an indication of sudden liquidity pressures or price premiums or similar stress points for gold ETFs. Why this move? Navneet Damani, senior group vice president and head of research for commodities and currency at Motilal Oswal Financial Services, pointed out that elevated global crude oil prices have put pressure on the dollar-rupee pair, the fiscal math, and the balance of payments. “If you can’t control crude oil imports, at least gold and silver imports could be curtailed,” said Damani. He noted that elevated import duties, which rose from 6% to 15% earlier, have not halted official and grey-market inflows. With the festive and wedding season (Navratri, Dussehra and Diwali) driving demand, restricting FoF inflows serves to limit foreign exchange leakage, aligning with Prime Minister Narendra Modi's appeal to defer discretionary gold purchases. “The reason behind the FoF stoppages is very simple: the government wants to curb demand because this is the festival and wedding season, to stabilize the Indian rupee,” said Pankaj Mathpal, founder and MD of Optima Money Managers. What investors should do Despite the gold FoF restriction, investors do not need to change their financial strategies. Damani highlighted that gold has corrected, building in negatives such as accelerating inflation and higher bond yields, making current levels reasonable for gradual accumulation. However, experts warned against buying out of fear of missing out. “Investment decisions should depend on requirements. It should not be FOMO because the government is stopping fresh investments into FoFs,” Mathpal advised. If your portfolio already holds sufficient gold, do not force additional purchases, he said, adding that those needing investment exposure can open a demat account to purchase gold ETFs directly on the exchanges or buy sovereign gold bonds (SGBs) in the secondary market. That said, investors should note that secondary-market SGB purchases no longer qualify for tax-free maturity gains, bringing in a 12.5% long-term capital gains tax, similar to that for gold ETFs. “For consumption needs like weddings, physical gold coins, bars, or jewellery remain fully accessible,” he said. Ultimately, investors can view this restriction as a regulatory adjustment and continue with their planned and goal-aligned allocation toward gold in their portfolio without overallocating to gold due to FOMO. docs.title: Pressing pause on the race to develop frontier AI isn't impossible—Here's what can be done
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Pressing pause on the race to develop frontier AI isn't impossible—Here's what can be done
 Barry Eichengreen , Will Fithian , Wesley Holliday 4 min read 20 Oct 2026, 02:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 Policy could exploit this industry’s big chokepoint of AI-chip supply to restrain its development beyond the limits deemed safe. Whether there should be a pause is for policymakers to decide. But they should recognize that it is feasible and, if implemented properly, likely to be sustainable. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Dario Amodei, a co-founder of Anthropic, among others, has warned that artificial intelligence (AI) poses an existential threat to humankind. Others have gone further and argued for pausing the training of new frontier AI models. 
 The counter-argument is that regulation, self-regulation included, is unlikely to be effective. And even if a pause is feasible in principle, there is little hope that it could be sustained in practice, given that the US and China desperately fear falling behind each other. 
 But a new report by an interdisciplinary group of researchers, of which we are members, concludes that a global pause on frontier AI training is both feasible and sustainable. If implemented appropriately, such a pause could continue for a decade or more, depending on factors such as the pace of gains in AI training efficiency. 
 Frontier models require AI chips whose supply chain is highly concentrated. A ‘hardwired pause’ would exploit this chokepoint by halting the production of training-capable AI chips. It would allow production of chips which are capable of fast AI inference on approved models, but which, owing to their design, cannot be practically used for training new frontier models. 
 Once production of inference-only chips ramps up, the pre-pause training-capable chips would be phased out, so they could not be used to fuel a renewed AI race . This hardwired pause would allow states to reap the economic benefits of AI inference without continuing AI training that may result in overwhelming disruptions to society and national security. 
 The supply chain for AI chips is highly bottlenecked. Advanced lithography (extreme ultraviolet) machines are available from just one supplier, the Dutch firm ASML, and ship in containers spread over 20 trucks and three cargo planes. ASML depends on mirrors from a single German high-precision optics firm, Zeiss. Refined rare earths are available from only a limited number of national sources. Other materials, such as high-purity quartz, come from a handful of locations. 
 As for the use of those chips, an evader using a single computer to train a small AI model may be impossible to detect. But hundreds of thousands of chips would need to be used for months or years at a time to train AI models at a scale significantly beyond that of current frontier models like OpenAI’s Astra. 
 After commandeering such a large hardware fleet, an evader would need to deceive the world for a long period into believing that the fleet was being used for, say, lucrative and computationally intensive inference. 
 This suggests that a limited number of interventions—including controls on the production and sale of training-capable chips, advanced lithography machines and rare earths—would go a long way toward supporting a pause in the training of frontier models. 
 This would still allow production of inference-only chips, such as certain model- specific integrated circuits that hardwire the architecture and weights of an approved model into the chip. 
 Model-specific chips already exist, but their economic attractiveness is limited by the high turnover of frontier models. Producing them would become more attractive with a pause on new frontier model training. 
 Some will object that pausing the production of training-capable chips will slow the advance of AI. That, of course, is the point. Still, with adequate cooperation it could be possible to construct internationally governed scientific preserves where training-capable chips could be used for declared, transparent research workloads.
 But could cooperation on a pause—between the US and China and more generally—be sustained over time? States could be tempted to defect from such an agreement, despite the risks, if the potential gains from AI advances are great, and hiding defection could become less difficult as training algorithms grow more efficient.
 But decision-makers should understand that they are engaged in a repeated game, and also that monitoring will occur and that immediate gains may be swamped by future losses if agreement breaks down. Adequate monitoring mechanisms can limit the risk of defection. The history of nuclear weapons containment suggests that an international agreement is worth trying.
 There are caveats, to be sure. Policymakers in the US and China may lack the patience needed to sustain cooperation over time. Given existing stocks of training-capable AI chips, countries might not sustain a pause unless a sufficiently comprehensive census is taken. Chip fabrication would have to be strictly monitored while developers of frontier models could become privileged monopolists unless regulation prevents them from exploiting their market power. 
 Whether the development of frontier AI should be paused is for policymakers to decide. But they should recognize that a pause is feasible and, if implemented properly, that it is also likely to be sustainable. ©2026/Project Syndicate 
 The authors are, respectively, professor of economics and political science, associate professor of statistics, and professor of philosophy, University of California, Berkeley.

docs.title: Who should be held liable for the harms of self-evolving AI? The answer is clear
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Who should be held liable for the harms of self-evolving AI? The answer is clear
 Rahul Matthan 5 min read 20 Oct 2026, 04:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 The law must keep up with AI which is delivering models that learn, adapt and evolve on their own. Labs have little control on how they are deployed. So, just as users of electricity are responsible for how it’s used, those who use continual learning models must be held liable for any resulting harm 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 In June last year, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology published a paper describing a process by which large language models could generate training notes and use them to update their own weights. 
 A one-billion-parameter model that could not solve a single puzzle in the test set managed to solve over 70% of them by using this technique. In a separate test, the notes a larger model wrote for itself proved better training material than those generated by GPT-4.1. 
 Today, AI models are trained by adjusting their weights on vast amounts of data until they perform as intended. The weights are then frozen, and the model released. From that point onwards, the model weights remain static—nothing that it encounters, not the documents we give it to read, nor the preferences we ask it to remember, is embedded in the model. 
 Since a model’s weights will not change once it is released, all our safety evaluations are conducted before that. This is also why regulators treat metrics such as the compute required to train a model or the number of parameters it contains as useful proxies for its capabilities. Once continual learning makes it possible for models to use their inputs to adjust their weights on the fly, all of this will have to change. 
 A model whose weights continuously change can soon become very different from the model that was released, so any evaluation conducted before release can only tell us what it could do on the day it was tested. Since small continuously trained models could quickly become far more capable than their size would suggest, while remaining well below any threshold that would bring them under scrutiny, our current approach to evaluating risk will no longer be useful. 
 Today’s frontier models are built like Swiss Army knives, packed with more knowledge and capabilities than any one user will need—because their makers can never know exactly how they will be deployed. 
 Continual learning allows us to build each model with basic capabilities that can be augmented by learning from the environments in which it is used. This will enable far greater efficiency, as each AI can excel only in the domain in which it is used, while more general capabilities irrelevant to its role fade away. 
 It is only a matter of time before AI labs ship such models. All that is holding them back from doing so already is probably concerns around safety. 
 Let’s consider how this would work in a law firm. 
 Today, law firms use general-purpose models to analyse their documents, hoping each time that the harnesses and workflows they have built will result in the correct outcome. A continual learning model, on the other hand, would ingest every opinion the firm writes, every transaction it structures and every correction a partner makes to an associate’s draft by adjusting its weights to reflect them. 
 Eventually, the model will represent the sum total of the judgement of the firm’s best lawyers, becoming better over time at working out what the law permits and where its edges lie than any general-purpose model could. 
 Any model continuously trained by a law firm could become exceptional at identifying loopholes in the law that criminals could exploit. Similarly, one that is continuously trained in a hospital would be outstanding at identifying treatments that could kill someone without being detected. Since all these nefarious capabilities are acquired post-deployment, our current approach to AI safety would be helpless to protect us from the harms that could result. 
 If this is the direction we are headed, we would do well to think through how these new risks can be mitigated. One side-effect of continual learning seems to be that the more a model’s weights are adjusted post-deployment, the more likely it is to ‘forget’ the safety guardrails embedded in it. 
 This is something model developers will have to address before they release these models to the public. But once they have done all that can be expected of them in that regard, the model builder should be protected from the harms that could result from what users do with it. 
 This approach is not unlike how we treat all providers of utility services. When electricity was first supplied to households, the wiring regularly gave people shocks, and, when badly laid out, set houses on fire. Yet no one held the power generation company responsible. 
 Over time, the law came to draw the line at the meter and the electricity company’s liability ended there. Everything beyond it—the wiring, the appliances and the uses they were put to—was the responsibility of the user household. 
 We need to apply the same rules to AI. Developers need to ensure that they have built guardrails that can endure the forgetfulness that is a normal side-effect of continual learning. Having done so, their liability should end at the meter. What happens beyond that as a result of what users choose to continuously train their intelligence on cannot be the responsibility of the provider of an intelligence model. 
 Deployers of continual learning models must be strictly liable for any resulting harm, regardless of the precautions they took. The liability should be serious enough that no one would use such a model without caution. This is what every government will need to do as AI becomes what Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor, in their 2025 essay, call a norm

Global 
 Autism-therapy workers say big chains pressured them to boost treatment hoursC
 Anna Wilde Mathews , Christopher Weaver , Tom McGinty , The Wall Street Journal 14 min read 21 Oct 2026, 06:47 AM IST 
 Summary
 Medicaid data show some private-equity-backed chains billed far more hours than rivals. Companies say patient needs guide treatment. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Minutes after an autistic 3-year-old lay her head on a Squishmallow stuffed toy and closed her eyes, Abigayle Hosking was ordered to take the makeshift pillow away and rouse the sleepy girl. The child was scheduled for four more hours of autism therapy at the Centria Healthcare clinic in Michigan where Hosking worked until last year.
 Hosking said she felt terrible. “The younger kids, you know, I think they need a break,” she said.
 Medicaid plans and private insurers will often pay for up to about 40 hours of autism therapy a week, and shut-eye doesn’t count. At Centria and some other large chains backed by private-equity investors, former employees said in interviews that they felt pressure to maximize therapy hours, claims the companies dispute.
 The Wall Street Journal analyzed the billings of five of the largest private equity-backed providers of autism therapy to Medicaid patients, including Centria. Together, the group’s average weekly therapy hours for those patients were 29% higher than competitors’ in 2024. All but one of those companies delivered more hours than local rivals.
 “It’s simple business math,” said Philip Painter, a physician who briefly served as chief medical officer at Centria. “You want to maximize the number of hours the child is doing.”
 Medicaid programs financed by state and federal taxpayers paid $10 billion for autism therapy last year, up from around $2 billion in 2021, driven in part by increasing numbers of treatment hours per patient.
 In autism therapy, treatment hours are supposed to be tailored to each patient’s needs, but there is debate about how much is warranted.
 Many autism-therapy providers and an industry group cite studies of young children showing high-hour therapy can help those with severe challenges. Government officials and insurers have scrutinized long hours, at times pointing to other research, disputed by some providers, that raised questions about the correlation between long therapy hours and improved outcomes. New federal guidelines for Medicaid say there is no correlation.
 Private-equity firms have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into building national chains of clinics to serve children diagnosed with autism. The Journal’s autism-treatment analysis looked at Centria, majority-owned by THL Partners; Action Behavior Centers, backed by Charlesbank Capital Partners; Hopebridge, acquired by Arsenal Capital Partners; Cerberus Capital Management-backed Lighthouse Autism Center; and Learn Behavioral, majority-owned by Gryphon Investors, which billed fewer hours a week, on average, than its competitors.
 All five companies said they individualize treatment, including weekly hours, based on patient needs, not financial considerations.
 The four companies with higher-than-average hours said the Journal’s analysis of Medicaid claims didn’t account for differences in the severity of patients’ autism, and that their nap policies aim to accommodate children’s sleep needs. Centria, Action and Lighthouse said their patients had more severe autism than average, justifying more therapy.
 Centria said waking a 3-year-old as described by Hosking wouldn’t have complied with its policies, and such an incident wasn’t documented at the time. Action disputed the assertion in the Medicaid guidelines that treatment intensity doesn’t correlate with outcomes.
 Former employees of the four higher-hour companies said in interviews they felt pressure to recommend long therapy schedules for children, and that centers sometimes turned away children who needed low weekly hours.
 The former employees said the companies applied the same approach to both Medicaid and privately insured patients.
 In Arizona, Centria billed 94% more hours a week per patient, on average, than competitors in 2024, and in Colorado, Action billed 81% more than local rivals, the Medicaid data show.
 LaDeana Thompkins’s son was scheduled for about 40 hours a week at an Action facility near Phoenix when she told the clinic in July that his hours would need to be cut by about half because he was starting kindergarten, according to emails reviewed by the Journal.
 In a meeting the next day, an Action staffer told Thompkins and her husband that their son wasn’t ready for kindergarten, and proposed that the boy, then 5, could delay going to school and continue full-time therapy, according to Thompkins and her husband, as well as documents from the time.
 The couple decided they didn’t want to hold off on kindergarten, where their son could get help from an aide and other support at their local school. The Action staffer told the couple that the clinic could accommodate the boy only if he was attending close to its recommended therapy hours, and that if he left and wanted to return, he might land on a waiting list, the Thompkinses said. “It felt like we just fell off a cliff,” LaDeana Thompkins said.
 Action’s chief clinical officer, Charna Mintz, said in an interview that if a family chooses school, “even if it is not what is clinically recommended,” the company would support the family in the transition. In a letter, lawyers for Action told the Journal the company had “information that would thoroughly debunk the narrative this patient is being used to support,” but couldn’t share it due to a healthcare privacy law.

docs.title: French protests can be traced to weak fiscal management—and therein lies a lesson
docs.text:
Opinion 
 French protests can be traced to weak fiscal management—and therein lies a lesson
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 21 Oct 2026, 07:31 AM IST 
 Summary
 The question that an over-indebted France must answer is whether its government can get its fiscal house in order. As credit gets costlier not just across the euro-zone but globally, fiscal responsibility assumes all the more importance. If at all, only the US can breathe easy. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 As student protests sweep across France, it is easy to dismiss it as familiar if uniquely French stuff. But at the bottom of it is something that’s increasingly common to governments all over: fiscal profligacy. 
 A redux of the Greek crisis of 2009-10 might seem distant, but as unrest spreads beyond French borders, it is time to examine if there are any lessons for us. 
 At the root of the problem is France’s inability to get its fiscal house in order. On the face of it, the protests echo concerns of India’s ‘cockroach’ stir over education: dilapidated classrooms, poorly run state schools, and so on. 
 But there the similarity ends. 
 Unlike in India, where years of lectures from multilateral institutions made economic policymakers wary of running high fiscal deficits, rich countries of the West had no such qualms. 
 Inevitably, the chickens are coming home to roost. Investors have begun treating France as the ‘sick man of Europe,’ with a debt-to-GDP ratio of almost 120% (in contrast with India’s 80% odd). 
 In France’s case, its yawning deficits and debt overload are chiefly an outcome of its inability to curb a rapidly rising pension bill. Paris has long been aware of this, but every time an administration tried to reform the system, it was forced to retreat. The net result is that many of its youth are condemned to a future of slower growth, strained public services and a welfare system far less supportive than it once was. 
 Add the country’s political chaos, with candidates on the far right and hard left vying to win its presidency next year, and the French stage seems set for months of turbulence that could spill across the wider euro-zone. 
 The question that France must answer—and a show of police force does not count as one—is whether it can exercise fiscal restraint. Consider: France’s budget deficit exceeds 5% of its GDP, which is more than India’s gap of 4.4% last year and this year’s target of 4.3%, and leaves very little space for finding extra cash to satisfy the needs of students. 
 As signs of discontent erupt in Belgium, Portugal, Spain and Albania, the EU could face a severe test. The EU’s Growth and Stability Pact, which limits national fiscal deficits to 3% of GDP, was designed partly for cohesion to enable a common currency, the euro. 
 Today, it exists only on paper, but the euro-zone has a unified monetary authority that recently hiked its policy rate to tackle inflation. Dearer credit affects all of Europe , but French bonds stand out for their rising yields and risk premia, which make it particularly expensive for Paris to borrow funds for public spending. 
 Given an oil shock amid an AI boom, costlier capital is a global trend. The US, whose debt pile has also grown enormous, has two key advantages. 
 One , its economy’s growth is robust—thanks largely to AI—and not weak like France’s. Two , the US dollar’s status as a trade and reserve currency spells vast global demand for its bonds, which lets America run outsized deficits year after year. Since this is not true of other countries, the sooner they recognize it and act accordingly, the better. 
 In any case, US yields have been hardening too, and it’s unclear if this is just a war blip, given how an AI investment cycle going beyond data centres could keep interest rates ‘higher for longer’ (if overall savings are unable to keep up). 
 With credit no longer cheaply available and the future uncertain on multiple fronts, no country can afford to relax its fiscal vigil.

 Snowy Alps, lakeside Airbnbs and road trips: an 8-day Swiss holiday for ₹1.5 lakh per person
 Shipra Singh 7 min read 20 Oct 2026, 01:52 PM IST 
 Summary
 A family of five from Noida spent ₹ 7.84 lakh on a winter holiday in Switzerland. Affordable flights, countryside Airbnbs, a rental car and home-cooked meals helped keep costs in check. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Switzerland may not be the first destination that comes to mind when planning a budget international holiday, but it is among the most sought-after destinations for a snowy winter getaway. Although wars, geopolitical tensions and rising airfares have made international travel more expensive, smart planning can still help keep costs in check. Travelling as a group, finding reasonably priced flights and making informed choices about accommodation, transport and food can help keep expenses in check, as a family of five from Noida discovered.
 Anu Arora, an education counsellor, and her family travelled to Switzerland in late December 2025 and spent ₹ 7.84 lakh, or about ₹ 1.57 lakh per person, on flights, accommodation, transport, food, sightseeing and other essentials. Although Christmas and New Year are peak tourist periods in Switzerland, the family found airfares from India relatively affordable.
 “When we compared destinations for our year-end holiday, flights to Switzerland were cheaper than to many other countries, at around ₹ 50,000-60,000 per person. These fares were broadly in line with our budget and about 35%-45% cheaper than summer rates,” she said.
 Beyond savings on flights, the family kept expenses in check by renting a car instead of relying on public transport, staying in countryside Airbnbs rather than hotels, and cooking most of their meals. These choices allowed them to enjoy a Swiss winter holiday without spending excessively on transport, restaurants and sightseeing.
 As part of Mint ’s travel series, Arora shares how her family planned its winter holiday in Switzerland, breaking down the costs and the choices that helped them save.
 Flights and visas
 We had visited Switzerland before, but never in winter. This time, we wanted to experience the snow-covered Alps and Christmas markets . Since both my children and daughter-in-law could take time off during the year-end break, we decided to travel together.
 While comparing destinations, we noticed that airfares to several countries were particularly high during the holiday period, whereas Switzerland was an exception. Direct Air India flights from Delhi to Zurich were available for about ₹ 50,000-60,000 per person, compared with around ₹ 80,000 per person in the summer months.
 We spent ₹ 2.68 lakh on return flights for five people, averaging ₹ 53,690 per person. Flights were our biggest single expense, accounting for about 34% of the total trip cost.
 Switzerland is expensive throughout the year, so we felt the additional cost of travelling during New Year was not substantial enough to change our plans. We applied for Schengen visas through VFS Global in New Delhi. Getting appointments was easy, and we received our visas within four days of applying. This was much quicker than what we would typically expect during the busy summer travel season. Only four of us needed visas, which cost us about ₹ 48,000, as one of us already had a Schengen visa.
 Prices across the major expense heads, including accommodation, transport and eating out, are similar in winter and summer, as both are peak tourist seasons. The additional expense we had to budget for this time was winter clothing. We spent ₹ 35,000 on winter jackets, snow boots and other winter gear purchased from Decathlon in India.
 Airbnbs and road trips 
 We chose Airbnbs in smaller towns over hotels in popular tourist destinations, as booking multiple hotel rooms for five adults would have been expensive. We spent ₹ 1.89 lakh on two apartments in Steinen and Sigriswil, averaging ₹ 27,000 per night for five people. Both had kitchens, which helped us save on food. Eating out was expensive: a meal for five cost around 90 Swiss francs ( ₹ 10,500), and finding vegetarian options was another challenge.
 Renting a car allowed us to stay outside the main tourist centres without worrying about access to public transport. We hired an automatic Nissan X-Trail SUV from Zurich airport for ₹ 1.25 lakh, including insurance. Fuel and parking cost another ₹ 19,600, taking our total transport expense to about ₹ 1.44 lakh, or ₹ 28,820 per person.
 In comparison, the Swiss Travel Pass, which offers unlimited travel on much of Switzerland's public transport network, would have cost us about ₹ 50,000 per person, or ₹ 2.5 lakh for the family. Renting a car saved us over ₹ 1 lakh compared with that option and gave us the flexibility to change our plans depending on the weather. Travellers comfortable driving a smaller or manual car can save further.
 After landing in Zurich, we drove straight to Steinen in central Switzerland, where we stayed for three days in a spacious three-bedroom apartment. From there, we explored Lucerne, Brunnen and Engelberg. We then moved to Sigriswil, a village overlooking Lake Thun, which served as our base for visiting Grindelwald, Lauterbrunnen, Mürren and Interlaken.
 Our second stop was Sigriswil, where we had booked an apartment through the local website e-domizil. This website sometimes has very good value-for-money listings, though using it is not very convenient.
 Our Sigriswil apartment had large windows overlooking the lake and a fireplace. We even watched the New Year's Eve fireworks from the apartment, enjoying the alcohol-free Champagne our host had gifted us, instead of spending on a celebration outside.

docs.title: 8th Pay Commission: What is gratuity, and how is it calculated based on last drawn salary? Expert explains
docs.text:
As employee unions continue to press for changes to the pay structure, gratuity and retirement benefits remain a key concern for central government employees nearing retirement.
Over the last few months, prominent unions have raised several demands before the panel on the fitment factor, revised basic salaries, allowances, gratuity limits and pension reforms. These include the National Council–Joint Consultative Machinery (NC-JCM) and the All India Defence Employees Federation (AIDEF). Proposals for a higher gratuity ceiling and revised retirement benefits are among those under discussion.
The unions’ core aim is to improve the livelihoods of serving employees and pensioners, and to secure a meaningful review of salaries after a decade. However, the final outcome will depend on the commission’s recommendations and the government’s decision.
 Gratuity is a lump-sum retirement benefit paid to eligible employees in recognition of their service. For central government employees, it is linked to emoluments and qualifying service. Under the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 2021, retirement gratuity is generally calculated at one-fourth of emoluments for every completed six-month period of qualifying service, subject to the prescribed maximum.
 Adhil Shetty, CEO of BankBazaar, explains, “Gratuity is a one-time lump sum paid to government employees at retirement in recognition of their years of service. It is calculated on the last drawn basic pay plus dearness allowance. For every six months of qualifying service, employees receive a quarter of this amount, subject to a ceiling of ₹ 25 lakh. Since gratuity is directly tied to basic pay, a higher revised basic under the 8th Pay Commission could raise payouts for employees retiring after its implementation.” 
 The central government constituted the 8th Pay Commission on 3 November 2025. It is a temporary three-member body headed by Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai, and will complete one year in a few weeks. Under its Terms of Reference (ToR), it has an 18-month mandate, and its report is expected by May-June 2027.
 Until the final report is submitted and the government announces its decision, all demands on gratuity, allowances and pensions remain proposals. Serving employees and pensioners should wait for official recommendations and implementation details before assuming any increase in retirement benefits. 
 Disclaimer: This article is for general information only. The final gratuity benefits will depend on the 8th Pay Commission’s recommendations and the government’s approval and implementation.

docs.title: Yes, the Fed can kill the AI boom
docs.text:
Global 
 Yes, the Fed can kill the AI boom
 Greg Ip , The Wall Street Journal 8 min read 20 Oct 2026, 05:25 PM IST 
 Summary
 Plus, AI slop comes for the government, why large families are a status symbol, and lessons from Jerome Powell’s calendar. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Back in 2000, as the Federal Reserve raised interest rates, entrepreneurs and investors surfing the internet wave insisted it didn’t matter. “Everybody knows the Fed’s going to raise rates in February, but as this comes closer, VCs are throwing ever larger amounts of money at us,” one told my then-colleague Jacob Schlesinger.
 We know what happened next. The Fed kept raising rates and the internet-stock bubble imploded.
 Déjà vu: The same arguments are being recycled today for artificial intelligence. What if “the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates because winning the race for super intelligence has a near infinite ROI,” hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman asked on X.
 John Arnold, co-chair of Arnold Ventures, argued higher rates could be “counterproductive” for inflation: They won’t reduce demand for AI inputs, but do “raise business operating expenses, some of which is passed along to consumers.”
 Let me set the record straight: The Fed is entirely capable of deflating the AI boom and inflation.
 Skeptics assume interest rates could only slow AI companies by raising their cost of borrowing. That is a fallacy. Short-term rates are the benchmark cost of liquidity, affecting overall financial conditions. With each successive increase, tighter credit ripples out along the risk spectrum, from Treasurys to corporate and household loans, equity and so on. The leveraged investors who buy risky assets see their funding squeezed. Appetites for initial public offerings, high-yield bonds, private credit and securitizations dry up.
 This is why asset meltdowns through history bear the Fed’s fingerprints: the 1929 and 1987 stock-market crashes, the dot-com and housing busts, emerging-market crises in 1982 and 1997-98. As assets deflate, investment follows and sometimes recession comes next. And with recession, inflation goes down.
 To be clear, the Fed doesn’t want to end the AI boom. It only wants overall inflation to fall to 2%, which doesn’t require that AI-related inflation do so as well.
 But make no mistake: If the only way to 2% inflation is to drain the lake of liquidity sustaining AI, the Fed has the means and, very likely, the will to do it.
 This is an edition of the WSJ Economics newsletter , your guide to the intersection of economics, markets and politics. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.
 What I’m Following
 Governments are “drowning in slop” thanks to AI, British writer Sam Freedman observes. From the U.S. to Europe and Australia, government agencies are seeing a sharp rise in requests for things like records or consumer complaints, presumably because chatbots have made it effortless to file forms. Governments are going to have to adjust. “Modern administrative states are built around processes that are difficult to use, often deliberately so, which helps ration demand,” Freedman writes. “AI blows this assumption apart.”
 The new American status symbol is a third child , writes Michael Konczal of the Economic Security Project. Analyzing a Fed survey, Konczal finds that nearly half of families with top-percentile incomes have three children or more. Among families just a bit less well off, only around 40% have at least three children. It is a sign of how rising costs for housing and child care are shaping family planning. In the past, it was lower-income families that tended to be larger. “This is [just] a correlation, but it’s the one you’d expect if money solves the hard parts of raising kids,” Konczal writes.
 Rising interest rates have pushed aside the trade war as global policymakers’ biggest anxiety, Harvard’s Jason Furman reports from the IMF meetings in Bangkok: “No one cares about tariffs anymore, they expect them to continue forever and have adjusted and moved on. Everyone cares a lot about high interest rates. They expect them to continue forever but they haven’t moved on. Oil prices fall somewhere between these two. Everyone cares some, aren’t sure if they’ll continue and have partially moved on.”
 Jerome Powell’s close relationships on Capitol Hill were no accident. As Fed chair, Powell held more meetings with political figures—mostly lawmakers—than his predecessors did, Thomas Drechsel of Johns Hopkins and Dali Tsakadze of the University of Maryland find, based on extensive study of recent Fed chairs’ public calendars. They also find that Fed chairs rely heavily on the central bank’s in-house economists, and that meetings with reporters have grown more common over the past 15 years.
 More From WSJ
 The immigration crackdown is exacerbating the housing shortage by making it harder to build. One builder in Florida said that wages for framers have roughly doubled to more than $40 an hour. “There’s no one lining up to do a lot of these jobs,” another said.
 Buying a laundromat isn’t the shortcut to the American dream that some social-media influencers portray.
 Voters in Alberta chose to stay in Canada by a convincing margin in a historic referendum. Ahead of the vote, Prime Minister Mark Carney used threats from President Trump to push for a new pipeline from Alberta to the west coast and other major infrastructure that could turn around Canada’s flagging productivity, I wrote last week.
 What to Watch
 Tuesday
 The final two-week sprint to the midterms begins. Traders on Kalshi like Democrats’ chances, giving them roughly 64% odds of taking back control of both houses of Congress as of Monday evening.
 8:30 a.m. ET: The Census Bureau publishes September housing-starts numbers. Economists polled by The Wall Street Journal are expecting to see a slight uptick

News India Inc braces for muted salary hikes in 2027 as costs rise, hiring slows Devina Sengupta 5 min read 20 Oct 2026, 04:22 PM IST Summary India Inc faces muted 2027 appraisals as geopolitical tensions, rising costs and weak festive demand restrain pay. While consultants project around 9% raises, recruiters expect rewards to favour top performers and AI-skilled talent, with one-time bonuses may increasingly replacing permanent hikes. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now India Inc is bracing for muted salary hikes in 2027 as rising costs, geopolitical uncertainty and a sluggish job market squeeze compensation budgets, with bigger rewards likely to be reserved for top performers, according to hiring experts. Higher crude oil prices amid the West Asia conflict, inflation that surged to a two-year high in September, the Reserve Bank of India’s rate increase and changing attrition trends are converging to complicate salary decisions. With consumer demand under pressure and businesses becoming more cautious about spending, companies are likely to exercise greater discipline in compensation budgets, even as they compete to retain critical talent. Consulting firms Deloitte and WTW (Willis Towers Watson) expect average salary increases to remain flat in 2027. Aon, meanwhile, projects nominal salary hikes of 9.1%, broadly in line with 2026, and real wage growth, adjusted for inflation, of 5.1%, from 4.3% in 2026. In banking, salary increases could average 6-7% in FY27, down from 8-9% in FY26, according to recruitment firm ABC Consultants. Employers typically roll out annual increments in April-May, though some do so a few months later. Work on salary hikes, promotions and bonuses, however, has already begun. Higher crude oil prices linked to the West Asia conflict are pushing up input costs and weighing on companies’ investment appetite. A subdued festive season, which runs from September to December and peaks around Diwali, adds to the concerns. “Three forces are converging: cost pressure from geopolitical conflict, attrition falling across every industry, and more Indian professionals returning home than leaving. Put together, they point to one outcome, which is that average salary increases in 2027 will flatline,” said Nitin Razdan, partner and human capital consulting leader for Deloitte South Asia. Razdan also told Mint that one trend in 2027 could be “one-time bonuses replacing permanent salary hikes”, as companies seek to reward employees without committing to higher fixed costs. Tighter budgets Consumers facing tighter budgets are delaying big-ticket purchases, with the effects likely to be felt over the coming quarters by companies in fast-moving consumer goods ( FMCG ), retail, e-commerce, logistics and other consumer-dependent industries. The information technology industry, too, reported a muted second quarter. Average salary increases peaked in 2022, when high attrition and the acceleration of digital adoption after the pandemic pushed companies to compete aggressively for talent. Since then, the employment market has seen ups and downs. According to Aon, attrition stood at around 18% in 2026, down from 21.4% in 2022. Employees in non-banking financial companies are projected to lead salary growth in 2027, with hikes of 10.1%, followed by energy at 9.9% and real estate and infrastructure at 9.8%. Inflationary pressures Recruiters, however, caution that these projections may be optimistic. “Inflationary pressures are likely to drive greater cost discipline across BFSI. Banking will see role rationalisation at senior and mid levels, particularly in operational and low-end tech roles. Salary increments are expected to average around 6-7%, compared with 8-9% in FY26, skewed towards top performers,” said Upasana Agarwal, partner, professional and financial services at recruitment firm ABC Consultants. Top performers, particularly those with AI skills, are still likely to command better rewards. Consulting firm WTW (Willis Towers Watson) said companies continue to differentiate compensation, directing higher investments towards employees with in-demand skills and critical talent. Aon estimates that top performers have received 2.24 times the variable pay and 1.85 times the salary increases of average performers. Senior management compensation typically includes a larger variable-pay component, linked to individual, team and company performance as well as market conditions. Variable pay can account for as much as 40% of overall cost to company (CTC). “We do not expect the broader macroeconomic environment, by itself, to materially alter salary increase budgets across all sectors. Industries such as Global Capability Centres ( GCCs ), Manufacturing and Pharmaceuticals are likely to maintain relatively stable increment levels, supported by ongoing investment and talent demand,” said Jude Vijay, rewards data intelligence leader, India, at WTW. “However, sectors that are more closely linked to consumer spending and global market volatility, including consumer products and retail, technology, and energy, may take a more cautious approach to pay increases depending on business performance and growth outlook,” Vijay added. docs.title: A marriage made in heaven: how the humble QR code met the small merchant
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 A marriage made in heaven: how the humble QR code met the small merchant
 Santanu Paul , B Sambamurthy 4 min read 20 Oct 2026, 12:41 PM IST 
 Summary
 UPI transformed merchant payments from a cash-and-change routine into a low-cost digital habit. As India reconsiders MDR, the challenge is to fund future innovation and cyber resilience without undermining adoption. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Can you remember the last time a shopkeeper handed you a toffee from a jar because they did not have small change? For decades, this was the norm at kirana stores and pharmacies across India. Today, that jar has all but disappeared. Some say an unintended consequence of the UPI revolution has been a secular decline in candy sales. That is partly because, over the past ten years, UPI has rewritten the payment experience for customers and merchants alike.
 The controversy over the return of the Merchant Discount Rate, or MDR, on UPI payments frames it as a consequential pricing question. But before arguing over who should pay for digital payments, it is worth revisiting how arduous person-to-merchant (P2M) payments once were, and how far India has come since UPI.
 In the toffee-jar era, small and micro-merchants operated in a cash-dominated world: managing change, maintaining handwritten accounts and making periodic bank visits. Customers without exact change altered their purchasing behaviour, sought store credit or accepted candies instead.
 To accept card-based electronic payments, merchants had to grapple with paperwork, point-of-sale machines, rental charges, connectivity issues and transaction fees. For large retailers, these costs were manageable. For tea sellers, vegetable vendors and tyre shops, however, digital payments were rarely worth the overheads.
 The QR breakthrough
 The technology to liberate small merchants arrived in India around 2015. The unsung hero of this story is surely Masahiro Hara, a Japanese engineer at Denso Wave, who invented the QR code in 1994. Hara was preoccupied with industrial parts tracking, and digital payments were farthest from his mind. Nevertheless, by the early 2010s, Chinese fintech companies such as WeChat Pay and Alipay had transformed QR codes into an ultra-frugal replacement for expensive merchant-side technology. All of a sudden, an inexpensive printed sticker could perform the core function of a costly point-of-sale terminal. Customers could scan QR codes with their phone cameras, enter the exact amount and pay with a gentle tap.
 The advent of QR codes made digital payment acceptance widely affordable for merchants of all stripes, but it also unleashed a world of fragmentation. Between 2015 and 2018, India was awash with proprietary QR codes. Merchants with Paytm QR codes could accept payments from customers using Paytm apps; the same story unfolded with many other closed-loop apps. Before long, merchants had to display a veritable garland of QR codes on their counters, one for each popular payment app.
 One code, many apps
 To counter the complexity of proprietary QR codes, two interoperable QR codes, UPI QR and Bharat QR, were launched in 2016 and 2017. Interoperable QR codes had the advantage of allowing merchants to accept payments from different payment apps using a common QR code. And yet, over the next three years, proprietary and interoperable QR codes lived cheek by jowl, competing to take market share from each other.
 In the end, an RBI expert committee led by Prof. Deepak Phatak of IIT Bombay recommended ending proprietary QR codes in 2020. Thanks to that intervention, most small merchants today receive payments from different UPI apps via a common UPI QR code designed by the National Payments Corporation of India, or NPCI . Chaos has made way for order.
 Today, the ubiquitous soundbox sits unobtrusively in most small stores, translating payment notifications into audible confirmations and allowing a street-side tea seller to serve her gaggle of customers without repeatedly checking her phone.
 Furthermore, digital collections are creating verifiable sales trails that lenders use to rate merchants and extend microcredit for working capital. Thanks to such merchant-focused innovations, India now has over 65 million merchants that accept UPI payments from over 500 million users. Contrast that with the decades it took India to install barely 10 million point-of-sale terminals.
 The MDR dilemma
 To MDR or not to MDR is a dilemma of Shakespearean proportions. As India debates a selective MDR regime, a 0.4% charge on eligible merchant payments above ₹ 2,000, capped at ₹ 300, which NPCI has just elected to postpone until after Diwali, the real question is whether this carefully designed fee corridor can pay for UPI’s future innovations and cyber resilience, while also enabling the system to encompass a billion citizens and 100 million merchants by 2030.
 Three decades after revealing the magic of the QR code and offering it to the world royalty-free, Masahiro Hara continues his work at Denso Wave. “I never thought it would be used as a form of money,” he said not long ago. “We do not receive a commission each time it is used.”
 Santanu Paul and B. Sambamurthy are the authors of Cashless Nation: How UPI Changed Everything, published by Penguin Random House. More on the book at cashlessnationbook.com
