docs.title: IMF outlook: How the latest forecast sends mixed signals on global growth
docs.text:
Opinion 
 IMF outlook: How the latest forecast sends mixed signals on global growth
 Niranjan Rajadhyaksha 4 min read 20 Oct 2026, 12:13 PM IST 
 Summary
 The International Monetary Fund's predictions are positive but the warning of its chief Kristalina Georgieva underscores serious risks for the world economy. There is a simple explanation for this gap. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The words of novelist George R.R. Martin made an unlikely appearance in a recent speech delivered by International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Kristalina Georgieva: “Winter is coming.” 
 This is the motto of the House of Stark in A Song of Ice and Fire novels written by Martin that were adapted for television later. It is also advice to get ready for hard times. Georgieva was thus sending a warning to prepare for a downturn. 
 Meanwhile, the organization she leads has released its latest estimates for economic growth in IMF member countries. It is a mixed bag. Global output is expected to grow by 3.1% in 2026, which is 0.4 percentage points lower than last year. Much of this is explained by slower growth in middle-income countries, especially China and India. 
 Yet, the new number is no different from the global growth forecast that the IMF had released in April. And the multilateral lender said global economic output next year will likely expand slightly faster than what it had expected six months ago. The West Asia war and the subsequent increase in energy prices does not seem to have done too much damage, at least for now. 
 There is a simple explanation for the gap between the word of caution that the IMF chief used and the numbers that IMF economists have released. Published forecasts usually report the central point in a range of possible outcomes emanating from statistical models, while speeches describe tail risks in uncertain times. Institutions that care for their credibility should sometimes warn rather than habitually cheer. 
 The global economy has been hit by multiple shocks after 2019—the pandemic, Russia-Ukraine war, US tariffs and the expanding footprint of the war in West Asia. However, despite all these convulsions, the current rate of global economic expansion is not too different from what it was in the seven years before the pandemic. The global economy’s resilience is noteworthy. 
 This resilience has come with costs. Any robust system needs buffers to help withstand shocks. The underlying reason is that stocks are less volatile than flows. The stability of a system depends on the size of a stock compared to the disturbance in a flow. The world used its strategic petroleum reserves to soften the blow from disruption of oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz. 
 Buffers eventually start to feel the pressure as well when the shock stretches out over time. Textbook macroeconomic shock absorbers are already under pressure. The ability of most countries to ease fiscal policy to support economic activity is now restricted by the escalating burden of public debt. And the ability to provide monetary stimulus through either lower interest rates or an expansion in central bank money has been upended by rising inflation. Resilience could be tested in the coming years. 
 The latest edition of the World Economic Outlook , the IMF’s biannual health report on the global economy, was written before the recent selloff in global technology stocks because of rising borrowing costs, hotter-than-expected US inflation data and growing scepticism over returns on massive infrastructure capital expenditures. One chart in the report distributes the economies of member countries along two axes—exposure to artificial intelligence (AI) and to rising energy prices. 
 A few years after the North Atlantic financial crisis of 2008, the IMF had mentioned the possibility of a two-speed global economy, depending on how badly a country was affected by the near-meltdown in the financial system. The multilateral lender has now used nearly identical language to describe the current situation—the language of winners and losers. 
 Some countries will be lifted by the boom in AI investments while others will be hit hard by the energy shock. The IMF has placed India in the quadrant comprising countries that could benefit from the integration of their trade with the AI technology cycle while being exposed to the deleterious effects of a further deterioration in their net energy exports. 
 One of the intriguing aspects of the new IMF report on the state of the world economy is that the effect of US tariffs on global economic growth has now been relegated to a less important position in its list of risks, much less than concerns about a further escalation in global energy prices or a sudden end of the AI investment boom. This is in stark contrast to what the IMF had said in October 2025, when tariff increases were the lead risk. 
 What happened? It is tempting to say that the world has learnt to live with higher tariffs. But the IMF says that court rulings and executive actions in the US have ensured that the US effective statutory tariff rate was about 5.3 percentage points below the level assumed earlier. 
 Meanwhile, a New York Federal Reserve study published on 8 October estimates that tariffs had added 2.9 percentage points to US inflation in a basket of goods by February 2026, which would otherwise have fallen by almost 1%. Significantly, the price increases were not restricted only to imported goods. They were seen in goods produced in the US as well. 
 Nobody should be surprised with these findings. 
 The author is executive director at Artha India Research Advisors.

docs.title: Dussehra 2026: 5 money rules to control spending and avoid debt
docs.text:
The festive season also brings attractive discounts on e-commerce platforms for mobiles, accessories, electronics, perfumes, clothes and more, which can lead to unplanned expenses. Easily available credit offers and loans add to the temptation, and without proper planning, such spending can strain household budgets and push families into debt.
The key is to plan festive spending and manage debt well in advance. This Dussehra, here are five practical personal finance rules to help you fully celebrate without compromising your long-term financial goals.
 The 50-30-20 rule is a simple and widely known budgeting method that can keep your finances in check during the festive season. Under this rule, 50% of your monthly income goes towards essentials such as groceries, rent and EMIs, 30% towards discretionary spending, and 20% towards savings. Festive shopping should come out of the 30% discretionary share, not the other two. 
 Keeping credit card utilisation at 30% or less helps you avoid overspending and keeps your debt in check. For example, if your credit limit is ₹ 3 lakh, try to keep the outstanding balance below ₹ 90,000. This approach supports a healthy credit profile and a high credit score.
 Set a clear festive spending limit and stick to it. Write down the figures, prepare a shopping list based on your actual needs, and track spending against it. The aim should be to end the festive season debt-free. 
 An emergency fund is essential for unforeseen events such as medical expenses, surgeries and accidents. Keep a dedicated fund equal to 3 to 6 months of your monthly expenses, and do not dip into it for festive spending. For example, if your monthly expenses are ₹ 1 lakh, set aside ₹ 3 lakh to ₹ 6 lakh separately.
 Automate your savings, mutual fund SIPs, fixed deposits and other investments so that they are debited from your bank account automatically. This builds discipline in both your daily finances and your investing, and helps create a healthy retirement corpus. If you are unsure, consult a certified financial advisor to plan your long-term investments. Do not postpone investments because of the festivities. 
 In summary, Dussehra is a festival that offers an opportunity to overcome unhealthy money habits, a lack of financial planning , and old patterns. It can provide them with a platform to celebrate the festival meaningfully while also managing finances responsibly. 
 Thoughtful spending, long-term planning, disciplined saving, and responsible credit use are key practices that can help an individual enjoy the festivities while keeping their financial future on track. 
 Disclaimer: This article is for general information only and should not be considered financial advice. Consider your financial circumstances and consult a qualified financial adviser before making financial decisions.

In a statement on 14 October, Fadnavis said that more than 85% of the state's talukas have been drought -hit. The government added 40 more regions to the list, taking the total affected sub-divisions to 305 out of 358, it added. As per the report, the direct transfer will be made to an authenticated list, which now includes an additional 3.5 lakh farmers. As per Fadnavis, the list has been processed to receive scheduled debt relief payments. According to the CM, drought is declared by November-end, and help is extended by December. However, the given the gravity of the situation, a notification was issued in October, he added. “This Diwali is going to be difficult for farmers. It will be difficult for them to manage during Diwali. Considering this situation, we have discussed and decided to provide assistance to farmers in the coming days. We have decided to give ₹ 5,000 to farmers as a Diwali bonus. This amount should reach the farmers' accounts before Diwali. The loan waiver amount is also being credited to their accounts,” Fadnavis stated. Earlier, Maharashtra Deputy CM Sunetra Pawar said the state was facing a severe drought and water crisis , adding that the government was “formulating” measures to address the situation and would extend assistance based on the recommendations of a Central government team assessing the drought-hit areas. News 
 How the Polycab case exposes the misuse of IBC for small dues
 Krishna Yadav 5 min read 20 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 Insolvency proceedings over minor vendor claims can exert commercial pressure on financially sound companies, even as courts warn against using the bankruptcy code as a debt-recovery tool. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Bankruptcy proceedings initiated by vendors and suppliers over unpaid dues from large companies are in focus after the insolvency court admitted a plea against wire and cable maker Polycab India on 7 October over an alleged operational debt of ₹ 2.79 crore claimed by supplier Asier Metals. 
 The admission raised concerns among bankruptcy lawyers, given Polycab’s strong financial position, with a net cash balance of ₹ 4,194 crore and shareholders’ net worth of ₹ 12,009 crore in FY26. On 9 October, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) stayed the admission order passed against Polycab by the Ahmedabad bench of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). 
 Insolvency experts said such cases highlight how proceedings can exert commercial pressure on companies even when the amount claimed is relatively small compared with their financial position. 
 “The case highlights an important concern in the existing IBC (Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code) framework. Even a financially sound company may find itself facing insolvency proceedings over a relatively small operational debt,” said Pooja Chakrabarti, partner at Argus Partners. 
 Amir Bavani, founder of AB Legal, Hyderabad, stated that the IBC was never intended as a debt-recovery tool, though it is frequently leveraged to compel companies into settling payments. 
 “While the inherent ethos of the code has always been to shun recovery tactics, it is true that IBC proceedings are more often than not employed as a pressure tactic to induce repayment,” Bavani said. 
 Under the IBC, an operational creditor can initiate insolvency proceedings for a default of at least ₹ 1 crore, subject to statutory requirements and the absence of a genuine pre-existing dispute over the debt. Operational creditors include suppliers, vendors and service providers, many of which are micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). 
 For listed companies, admission into the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) can trigger regulatory disclosures and affect investor confidence, lender relationships and business operations. 
 “The possibility of insolvency proceedings being used as leverage in commercial payment disputes is a legitimate concern. The consequences of admission can create substantial commercial pressure on a corporate debtor to settle outstanding claims, even where the amount involved is relatively modest,” said Vidya K., partner at King Stubb & Kasiva. 
 A Polycab spokesperson said in response to Mint's queries, "We do not expect any adverse/material impact on financial or business operations arising from the said order. We continue to hold a zero-debt position with the cash/investment liquidity and our balance sheet remains strong with net cash position in excess of Rs.4,000 crore and net worth of ₹ 11,682 crores as per the audited financial statements for FY26. We remain focused on our business operations and are committed to conducting them with the highest standards of transparency, integrity , and governance.” 
 The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India and the MSME ministry are yet to respond to Mint’s queries. 
 Legal limits 
 Data from the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India show that operational creditors had initiated 4,162 insolvency proceedings as of 30 June 2026. Of these, 893 were withdrawn, 930 were closed following appeal, review or settlement, 452 resulted in approved resolution plans, and 1,271 led to liquidation. Another 616 remain ongoing. 
 Courts have also cautioned against using the IBC merely to recover money. In April 2026, the Supreme Court said while hearing Anjani Technoplast Ltd v. Shubh Gautam that the insolvency process “must be reserved for cases of genuine insolvency or financial distress, not for the enforcement of money decrees”. The case concerned a financial creditor’s petition under Section 7 of the IBC. 
 In May 2025, the NCLAT dismissed an appeal by supplier SNJ Synthetics against PepsiCo India over alleged dues of about ₹ 1.97 crore, including interest, holding that the IBC could not be used as a debt-recovery tool in the circumstances.
 Yogendra Aldak, executive partner at Lakshmikumaran & Sridharan, said listed companies should respond promptly to insolvency proceedings, maintain documentation of disputed claims and take timely legal action, including appeals where warranted. 
 For smaller businesses, delayed payments can threaten day-to-day operations as suppliers struggle to meet wages, financing costs and production expenses. Insolvency proceedings can bring their grievances against large buyers into focus, but do not guarantee recovery. 
 “For a small business, ₹ 2 crore to ₹ 5 crore can mean its entire working capital, wages, bank repayments and ability to continue production,” said Vinod Kumar, president of India SME Forum. 
 “For an MSME, initiating insolvency proceedings does not guarantee payment. The supplier may incur legal costs and face delays, and ultimately recover less than the amount owed. At the same time, the buyer and its wider supplier network can face substantial disruption. The IBC is a consequential legal remedy, not a guaranteed debt-collection strategy,” Kumar added. 
 Policy reforms 
 To address such disputes, the government amended the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006, via the Amendment Act, 2026, passed in August. The updated legislation establishes strict timelines for mediation and arbitration , introduces online dispute resolution, and strengthens the enforcement of settlements and

Rising car prices and aspirational consumer choices are driving higher auto loan sizes, according to TransUnion CIBIL’s ‘Shifting Gears 2026 – Credit Drives Today’s Mobility’ report.
Among the demographics, Gen Z and younger Millennials are more visible among first-time car buyers widening the mobility credit market and increasing the role of formal credit in enabling mobility across India, it said.
It noted that between H1FY19 and H1FY26, the average passenger vehicle loan amount grew by 49% to ₹8.2 lakh, average loan tenure increased by five months to 62 months, and 51% of higher-value car loan borrowers were from semi-urban and rural India.In the same period, two-wheeler loans became a mainstream credit product, implied by the composition of first-time borrowers who have over two years of credit history: 43% in 2026 vs 27% in 2019. Further, non-banking finance companies (NBFCs) continue to lead vehicle financing, accounting for 73% of two-wheeler loans and 37% of passenger vehicle loans, it added.Two-wheelers closely linked with how young India studies, works, earnsAccording to Bhavesh Jain, MD and CEO of TransUnion CIBIL, two-wheelers are closely linked with how young India studies, works and earns. “For a student travelling to college, a young professional commuting to work, or someone earning through the gig economy or pursuing an entrepreneurial opportunity, personal mobility can open up a much wider set of possibilities,” he said.Further, Jain noted that the borrower behind a two-wheeler loan is also changing. “More consumers are coming in with an established credit history, and many continue to build wider credit relationships after the vehicle purchase. Two-wheeler finance is increasingly becoming part of a longer customer journey, with relevance extending well beyond the initial mobility need,” he added.Two-wheeler loans, traditionally seen as consumers’ first credit product, have now graduated into a mainstream credit product.Two-wheeler loans have moved beyond their traditional role as an entry point into formal credit ecosystem. First-time borrowers accounted for 39% of two-wheeler loan originations in H1 2026, down 19 percentage points from 2019, with their share declining from the pre-pandemic period.However, 43% of borrowers had more than two years of credit history at the time of origination, up 16 percentage points from 2019. This changing mix shows a growing share of credit-experienced consumers participating in the two-wheeler loan market.In H1 2026, 64% of borrowers for two-wheelers were from semi-urban and rural geographies (SuRu), and 43% were aged 30 years or younger.PV purchasers prefer SUVs, feature-rich vehiclesThe report also noted that passenger vehicle financing is increasingly reflecting a shift towards higher-value purchases. Preference for SUVs and feature-rich vehicles has contributed to higher vehicle prices and premiumisation, making financing more central to car ownership.The average passenger vehicle loan amount reached ₹8.2 lakh in H1 2026, up 49% from H1 2019, while the average repayment tenure increased by five months to 62 months.NBFCs) continue to hold the largest share of passenger vehicle loans at 37%, ahead of private banks at 26%, with an increase in share of 4 percentage points from 2019 to 2026.The active passenger vehicle borrower base reached 2.5 crore as of June 2026, 1.7 times the June 2019 level. Portfolio quality improved over the same period, with 90+ days past due balance-level delinquency declining by 95 basis points to 0.5%.Gen Z, younger Millennials more visible among first-time car buyersThe report added that consumers are taking different routes into car ownership. Gen Z and younger Millennials are more visible among first-time car buyers and consumers moving from two-wheelers to cars, while core and older Millennials are increasingly represented among repeat buyers and consumers financing higher-value vehicles.These shifts are also reaching wider markets.Rural originations among consumers moving from a two-wheeler to a car grew at a 15% CAGR since 2019, almost twice the 8% CAGR for overall auto-loan originations.Premiumisation is extending beyond metros too, with 51% of borrowers taking another higher-value car (HVC)2 loan in H1 2026 going to consumers in semi-urban and rural geographies, up six percentage points since 2019.“Car ownership is increasingly being shaped by a combination of aspiration and affordability. Consumers are choosing higher-value and feature-rich vehicles, while larger loan amounts and longer tenures are helping make these purchases more manageable,” Jain noted.He added that premiumisation extending beyond the larger cities, reflects how ownership aspirations are changing across India.Disclaimer: This story is for educational purposes only. docs.title: Building India’s deep-tech enterprise pipeline: from IP to IPO
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Building India’s deep-tech enterprise pipeline: from IP to IPO
 Padmaja Ruparel 12 min read 21 Oct 2026, 08:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 Capital is only one component of enterprise creation. Entrepreneurs need mentors versed in science and markets, industry partners to test technology, specialised labs, help with regulatory approvals and standards, and tech-transfer offices that protect intellectual property (IP). 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 As entrepreneurial energy plays an ever-larger role in India’s success story, we present a package of weekly opinion articles by members of TiE, a global organization for startups and entrepreneurs. From the rural reach of India’s startup revolution and the easing of capital and compliance challenges to the role of angel investors, how startups and micro, small, and medium enterprises must grow together and how best to track innovation, TiE authors cover a wide spectrum of relevant issues. 
 ***
 India’s startup ecosystem is entering a more challenging phase. The focus is shifting from counting startups, patents or funding rounds to evaluating how many Indian technologies move from lab validation to global markets and become established, publicly accountable enterprises.
 Beyond the startup count
 India has demonstrated significant progress in fostering startups. As of March, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) had recognized as many as 223,000 startups. Over 13,000 new patent applications were filed by startups, but many were abandoned and only 2,174 were granted. The moot point is that once filed, is the patent for technology differentiation really followed up to create a product for commercialization? Most of these intellectual properties (IPs) are viewed as a “protection” rather than “assets”. And that’s moot in today’s fast-evolving, technology-led world.
 Today, nearly 92% of the market capitalization of the S&P 500 is derived from intangible assets—brands, IP, software and data—up from just 17% in 1975. Global spending on intangible investment has crossed $4.7 trillion a year in advanced economies, overtaking investment in physical infrastructure. This is one of the most significant shifts in modern economic history: the countries that lead are no longer those with the largest industrial base, but those that own the world’s most valuable IP and brands. India’s next chapter will therefore be defined not by “Make in India,” but by the ambition to own the world.
 India’s real gap is the gap from research to IP, then to products, companies and global scale. Deeptech startups build on scientific breakthroughs in fields like materials, semiconductors, biotech, space, robotics, energy and quantum computing—domains where the IP is not adjacent to the business; it is the business itself. Therefore, the better measure of success is whether a startup becomes a professionally managed enterprise that outlasts its founders.
 Deeptech changes the equation
 This dynamic creates a fundamentally different development trajectory. Deeptech companies may require several years to transition from laboratory research to commercial scale and face numerous risks. Scientific concepts may not prove viable, and technologies that succeed in laboratory settings can fail in practical applications. Securing regulatory approvals and certifications often requires several years, and customer adoption of new technologies may be slow. These firms typically require multiple funding rounds before generating substantial revenue, thereby increasing capital risk.
 Applying expectations of rapid revenue growth, as seen in software companies, can result in premature down-rounds, underinvestment or the abandonment of strategically significant technologies. The implication is evident: deeptech sectors demand not only patient capital but also enduring institutional support, testing facilities, early customers and constant strategic guidance.
 What global firms reveal
 The most instructive global examples extend beyond narratives of venture funding. They show that deeptech companies are built through coordinated systems spanning research, infrastructure, customer engagement, manufacturing partnerships, long-term technical roadmaps, building talent and, of course, funding.
 IBM aims to deliver a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029 and is pursuing interim demonstrations of quantum advantage. The lesson: breakthrough technologies attract investment when progress is shown as clear, measurable technical milestones, not vague promises of future disruption.
 Emerging artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure firms are commercializing via distribution partnerships. For example, Fundamental raised funding while securing deployment through Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure and customer channels. For Indian deeptech firms, the central question extends beyond funding. It is critical to understand the need for institutions that can facilitate the achievement of technical, industrial and commercial milestones, and the ways through which they can do so.
 The bridge is more than money
 Over two decades of India’s startup journey, one lesson is clear: capital is only one component of enterprise creation. Entrepreneurs need mentors versed in science and markets, industry partners to test technology, specialized labs, help with regulatory approvals and standards, and tech-transfer offices that protect IP, forge industrial ties, support spin-outs and negotiate founder-friendly licences—plus early-adopter customers and investors.
 India needs to move beyond a narrow focus on patent counts. A patent may be legally valid yet commercially insignificant. For deeptech firms, the most valuable IP often extends beyond the patent itself—to proprietary algorithms, industrial designs, scientific datasets, differentiated know-how and trusted brands. Wi

docs.title: Delhi smog: Why satellites and machinery are unlikely to solve the problem—and what actually might
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Delhi smog: Why satellites and machinery are unlikely to solve the problem—and what actually might
 David Fickling 4 min read 20 Oct 2026, 03:30 PM IST 
 Summary
 For years, the government has been trying to curb the burning of rice straw on farms around India’s capital. First by offering seeders, then by using satellites to tip off local officials on illegal fire hotspots. But policymakers can't use technocratic solutions to fix a political economy problem. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Launched around the turn of the millennium, Nasa’s Terra and Aqua satellites have served as workhorses of climate observation for decades. From 700km above Earth, they track clouds, algae, forests, smoke plumes and fires, producing some of the most iconic images ever captured from orbit. 
 Yet farmers in India have been thwarting these sophisticated eyes in the sky with techniques that have barely changed since the Stone Age. That helps explain why technocratic efforts to tackle Delhi’s chronic air pollution keep falling short. 
 It would be comforting to think that better regulation and its implementation could clear the apocalyptic haze that descends on Delhi every winter. The harder truth is that until the political and economic incentives behind the pollution change, choking smog will remain an annual blight. 
 Satellites once seemed to offer part of the solution. One significant source of Delhi’s seasonal pollution is farmers burning rice straw after the monsoon harvest to clear their fields for the winter wheat crop. Haryana, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh, the states surrounding the capital, produce about a quarter of India’s rice. Since 2021, government authorities have been trying to use satellites to tip off local officials on illegal fire hotspots and send enforcement crews. 
 But t​​​​​​he initiative ran headlong into an adage known as Goodhart’s law: Once a measure becomes a target, people learn how to game it. 
 The satellites only pass over northern India in a brief window of the day, between 10am and 2pm. A 2024 India Today investigation found that government officials in Punjab were tipping farmers off about the schedule, allowing them to shift their burning later in the day. 
 The result was revealing. The number of large farm fires occurring after 3pm in the state went from about 3% in 2021 to more than 90% in 2024 and 2025. 
 We’ve seen this movie before. The stick of satellite surveillance was developed in part because an earlier technocratic carrot had failed. 
 In the late 2010s, officials hoped that mechanized equipment could eliminate the need for stubble burning. Tractor-drawn machines such as the Happy Seeder and Super Seeder, which allow farmers to sow wheat directly into fields without first burning the rice residue, were touted as a way to curb smog, boost yields and modernize Indian agriculture. 
 That didn’t work. Farmers who switched to seeders had to pay for the machinery, and diesel to power it. Poorer farmers relying on community-owned equipment may have to wait their turn during a narrow planting window when every lost day costs money. 
 Against the speed and simplicity of dropping a match, machinery struggled to compete. About a quarter of the crop-residue machines distributed in Punjab since 2018 are out of action. Even among farmers who use them, about half still burn stubble. 
 The root of the problem lies in the political economy of Indian agriculture. The government has made growing rice extraordinarily attractive in northern India, with guaranteed floor prices, near-unlimited procurement and subsidies for water pumping and fertilizer. 
 Those incentives encourage farmers to produce vast quantities of a crop that leaves them with an equally large amount of residue to clear in a hurry. Against such powerful economics, Happy Seeders and satellite surveillance never stood much of a chance. 
 Prospects for change are about as gloomy as Delhi’s skies during Diwali . Decades of effort to shift India’s rice and wheat bowl away from Punjab and Haryana towards eastern states have barely dented paddy cultivation near the capital. Attempts to persuade farmers to switch to less environmentally damaging crops such as corn and lentils have fared little better. The result is a paradox: India keeps encouraging farmers to grow rice beyond the needs of its 1.4 billion people. Government inventories have swelled to record levels this year: 10 times above the required buffer. 
 The clearest sign that Delhi is on a path to cleaner air would be a decline in the amount of paddy grown nearby and therefore the acreage liable to be burnt each year. Instead, the numbers are moving in the opposite direction. And the political obstacles to changing that are formidable. The last serious attempt to overhaul India’s agricultural system, in 2020, brought farmers from the northern states onto the streets around the capital for a year, until the government eventually backed down. 
 That’s the trap. Officials keep reaching for technological fixes since the underlying political problem is so difficult to confront. But the metric that matters isn’t how many fires satellites detect or how many seeders governments distribute. It’s how much paddy farmers plant. Until that acreage starts shrinking, no amount of technology will clear Delhi’s skies. ©Bloomberg 
 The author is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering climate change and energy .

Global 
 Trump promises cash and bailouts to woo midterm voters worried about high prices
 Marianne LeVine , Natalie Andrews , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 21 Oct 2026, 06:44 AM IST 
 Summary
 The president has laid out plans for an $8 billion bailout for farmers as voters raise concerns about costs. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 $5,000 for every American adult. An $8 billion bailout for farmers. $90 payments for seniors.
 President Trump is relying on a new strategy to salvage Republican seats in the midterm elections: promising an array of financial benefits to Americans, some of which he said he would only deliver if his party defies the polls and keeps control of Congress.
 The president started his campaign to put cash in the pockets of voters during Republicans’ midterm convention in September, when he announced a $1 trillion proposal to send $5,000 to each adult citizen—if the GOP holds on to its congressional majority. Since then, Trump has sent $90 to Medicare recipients to offset premiums and $500 checks to nearly one million people for what the administration called excessive fees under the Affordable Care Act.
 On Monday, Trump said he would send $8 billion in direct payments to U.S. farmers, some of whom have soured on the president amid his tariffs and as prices for diesel, gasoline and fertilizer have risen since his war with Iran. And on Tuesday, the president announced a new program that would provide up to $30,000 to Americans if they report a tip about government fraud.
 The White House is also discussing rolling out executive orders in the remaining days before the midterms aimed at addressing high prices, including one focused on reducing housing costs, according to people familiar with the matter.
 Republicans are facing one of the toughest midterm environments of any party in years, and the series of policy announcements serve as both an effort to motivate voters and a tacit acknowledgment that people are hurting financially. Democrats have accused the president of trying to buy votes.
 Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, described Trump as the “unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party,” and said that “the choice has never been clearer: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, common-sense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”
 The pledges get cheers at rallies where Trump supporters don red hats and wait in long lines to get a prime spot, but it is unclear if they will turn out the voters that Republicans need, those who vote conservative but tend to stay home during elections when Trump isn’t on the ballot.
 A Wall Street Journal poll last month found that voters aren’t sold on Trump’s proposed $5,000 checks, with 64% of respondents calling it a bad idea.
 Trump outlined the $8 billion farm bailout during a rally Monday in Kansas, telling his supporters that the Agriculture Department would launch a “Harvest Fuel Relief program” that would help offset rising diesel costs as farmers harvest their crops.
 “And when the Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers,” Trump said at the rally.
 Trump also said he would sign legislation permitting the year-round sale of gasoline blended with 15% ethanol, a long-sought-after policy by U.S. corn growers. Congress has to first pass the legislation, which faces an uphill climb. Trump said he would only agree to the policy if Republican Sen. Roger Marshall wins in Kansas against Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton.
 “With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E-15 permanent,” Trump said. “But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it.”
 The president has also made several announcements about new projects that are intended to benefit states that will help determine which party controls Congress. The president last week wrote on social media that Taiwan had committed to buy natural gas from a proposed export terminal in Alaska. ​​And he highlighted a Minnesota company’s plan to build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa.
 During a House Finance Committee hearing in September, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent answered questions about President Trump’s plan to pay each adult citizen $5,000 if Republicans win the midterm elections. Photo: Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg News
 Some of the benefits have already been distributed to voters. The $500 Affordable Care Act refund checks went out on Oct. 1 (alongside a letter touting his record on cutting healthcare costs), and the $90 payments to Medicare recipients were deposited in bank accounts or sent out on Oct. 8.
 But the president’s proposal to dole out $5,000 checks to Americans, which Trump has said would be contingent on the GOP keeping control of Congress, is expected to face hurdles. Democrats and some Republicans have expressed skepticism, raising concerns that such a move would balloon budget deficits and fuel inflation. Sending $5,000 to every American adult would likely cost well over $1 trillion, the Journal has previously reported.
 The federal government has made direct payments to Americans in the past. In the 2020 election, as Trump was running for re-election and the Covid pandemic ravaged the country, the government sent out $1,200 checks to tens of millions of Americans that arrived signed by Trump with letters from the White House taking credit for a bipartisan deal passed by Congress.
 In 2022, then-President Joe Biden said he would forgive up to $20,000 in federal student loan debt for tens of millions of Americans. Conservatives dismissed the move as an attempt to win over young voters ahead of that year’s midterm elections. Democrats lost nine seats in the House and gained one seat in the Senate.
 Democrats say Trump’s proposals won’t move the needle in this year’s midterms, where concerns about affordability are top of mind for voters.

docs.title: New UN initiative will aim to tackle military uses of AI
docs.text:
The initiative by the UN Institute for Disarmament Research plans to launch Thursday, establishing the first international forum for key players to try to tackle the issue.
Robin Geiss, head of the Geneva-based institute known as UNIDIR, warned at a UN press conference on Tuesday that "the margin for human judgment is increasingly narrow, including in the nuclear domain".
It's difficult to assess how close the world is to machines possibly acting outside of human control, Geiss said, and that uncertainty "is the issue we're trying to resolve here".
One problem is that AI is increasingly creeping into so many areas - early warning systems, information gathering and reconnaissance, to name a few - "and it's quite difficult to say at which point we're actually really losing control", he said.
For a long time, he said, there was widespread reluctance to deal with AI guardrails, but the proliferation of its capabilities and the potential impact have led to "a growing realisation that we stand at a crossroads - that now is the time to act, including on military AI".
Geiss said the UN recognises that global competition to lead on AI poses serious obstacles.
"But concerns about AI's impact are already transcending geopolitical blocs, and they're prompting action from major powers," he said, pointing to a proposal last month for the US and China to set up an AI safety alert system for issues that could threaten national security.
The risks posed by AI were a major topic in speeches by leaders of many of the UN's 193 member nations at their annual high-level meeting last month.
UNIDIR this summer established a Center of Excellence on AI, Peace and Security, the first permanent platform by the world body focused on those issues. Geiss said it received funding from all five major nuclear powers - the US, Russia, China, Britain and France.
On Thursday, UNIDIR will launch a new forum as part of the centre to bring together "actors from every relevant sector and all over the world" to work on AI in military uses.
Geiss was vague on exactly what the initiative will do, but he said it will be part of other AI efforts being launched by the centre this week. Another will focus on the role of industry and aims to develop "a framework for responsible industry behaviour", he said.
Decisions by companies on design and development "determine whether AI-enabled military capabilities are ultimately reliable, predictable and whether they can operate in line with international law", Geiss said.
For that reason, he said, UNIDIR is developing a framework of responsible industry behaviour that will "provide practical, voluntary guidelines" that follow international law and ensure human rights.
The UN agency will hold consultations this week with defence technology companies, software developers, subcontractors, investors and others that will work alongside governments, civil society, academia and experts, Geiss said.
UNIDIR is also launching an initiative focused on the risks of AI misuse by armed groups, he said, warning that such actors are already using the technology to support operational planning, execution and logistics.
"The urgent issue of AI in the military domain will certainly no longer be allowed to linger in the shadows," Geiss said. "The time has come to pull our strengths and confront AI in the military head-on." (AP)

Anand James, Chief Market Strategist, Geojit Investments Limited NCC LTP: ₹128 View: Buy Target: ₹137 SL: ₹123 NCC is showing early signs of a recovery after a prolonged corrective phase. On the daily chart, the stock has broken above its declining trendline, indicating an initial shift in the short-term price structure. Momentum is also improving, with the MACD crossing above its signal line, while the RSI has recovered from the oversold region, suggesting selling pressure is easing. On the weekly chart, the recent candle formation resembles a Morning Star reversal pattern, pointing to buying interest emerging near lower levels. The combination of improving momentum and a trendline breakout strengthens the possibility of a short-term rebound. As long as ₹123 holds, the recovery setup remains valid, with potential for a move towards ₹137 over the next few weeks. CHECK Stock Market LIVE Updates 
 J&K Bank LTP: ₹139 View: Buy Target: ₹154 SL: ₹132 J&K Bank is showing early signs of recovery after finding support near its 200-DMA, with the latest price action indicating renewed buying interest. A strong bullish Marubozu candle has emerged from the support zone, improving the prospects of a near-term reversal. Momentum is also beginning to stabilize, with the MACD histogram flattening after a period of weakness, suggesting that selling pressure is gradually fading. The stock is also nearing a PSAR breakout, which, if confirmed, could further strengthen the short-term recovery setup. The broader structure remains constructive as long as the 200-DMA continues to provide support. A sustained move above the immediate resistance zone could attract further buying and pave the way towards 154 over the next few weeks. The bullish setup remains valid above ₹132, which should be maintained as the stop-loss level. VRL Logistics LTP: ₹287 View: Buy Target: ₹309 SL: ₹276 VRL Logistics is showing signs of renewed strength after forming a bullish reversal candle following the recent consolidation. The stock has reclaimed its 20-DMA and moved above the middle Bollinger Band, suggesting that near-term momentum is shifting in favour of buyers. Momentum indicators are also improving. The MACD is approaching a bullish signal crossover, while the SMIO histogram is printing shorter negative bars, indicating that selling pressure is gradually fading. The broader price structure remains constructive following the strong recovery from the July lows, with the recent consolidation holding above important support levels. A sustained move above the nearby resistance zone could trigger the next leg of the recovery. As long as ₹276 holds, the bullish setup remains intact, with potential for a move towards ₹309 over the next few weeks.

Cost pressures to persist for cement major UltraTech in the near term
 Demand is expected to pick up from mid-November, after the festival season. Urban housing, infrastructure and private-sector capex are likely to remain key growth drivers
 premium 
 UltraTech has extended its lead in cement capacity and market share while maintaining its cost leadership and strong cash flow generation
 Devangshu Datta 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 11:08 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Cement major UltraTech’s September quarter (Q2FY27) results indicate that it retains its leadership in a crowded market. Volumes grew 13 per cent year-on-year (Y-o-Y), while the company continued with its planned capacity expansions. Although the monsoon season is typically weak for cement demand, price hikes helped support realisations to some extent. However, rising costs continued to weigh on profitability.
 Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) per tonne dropped to ₹240 quarter-on-quarter (Q-o-Q) to ₹974. Going ahead, high fuel costs remain a key concern, although operating leverage and strong volume growth could provide some relief. Margin recovery will also depend on maintaining prices in a competitive market. UltraTech added 4.6 million tonnes (mt) of cement capacity by September 2026, taking its domestic capacity to 204.7 mt.
 The company launched its cables and wires (C&W) business, UltraVolt, in September. It has already committed ₹1,100 crore of the planned ₹1,800 crore capital expenditure (capex), which is expected to be completed in the second half of FY27. The C&W distribution network includes more than 80,000 retailers and electricians across 500 districts and 15,000 pin codes. More than 1,500 channel partners have also signed up to become UltraVolt dealers.
 UltraTech’s Q2FY27 earnings were in line with consensus estimates. Consolidated revenue rose 19 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹23,300 crore, while Ebitda grew 20 per cent to ₹3,700 crore. Ebitda per tonne increased 7 per cent Y-o-Y, while declining ₹240 Q-o-Q to ₹974. The operating profit margin (OPM) expanded 20 basis points Y-o-Y to 16 per cent. Adjusted net profit rose 22 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹1,500 crore.
 Management remains confident about medium-term cement demand. Prices strengthened in September and October, although cost pressures persist. The company is also considering expanding beyond its planned capacity of 240 mt per annum (mtpa) by FY28, with detailed plans for further expansion likely to be announced by the end of FY27. Meanwhile, it is scaling up its nascent C&W business.
 Cement sales volume rose 13 per cent Y-o-Y to 38.2 mt, while blended realisation increased 5 per cent to ₹6,095 per tonne, up 2 per cent Q-o-Q. Ready-mix concrete (RMC) revenue grew 29 per cent Y-o-Y, while white cement revenue rose 4 per cent. However, operating expenditure per tonne increased 5 per cent Y-o-Y and 8 per cent Q-o-Q, driven by higher fuel and freight costs. Depreciation and interest costs rose 6 per cent and 20 per cent Y-o-Y, respectively.
 In H1FY27, revenue grew 17 per cent Y-o-Y, while Ebitda and net profit increased 16 per cent and 18 per cent, respectively. OPM contracted 20 basis points Y-o-Y to 18 per cent, while Ebitda per tonne rose 3 per cent to ₹1,099. Operating cash flow (OCF) stood at ₹6,910 crore, compared with ₹5,570 crore in H1FY26. Capex was ₹5,770 crore, resulting in free cash flow of ₹1,140 crore, against ₹770 crore a year earlier. Net debt increased to ₹23,500 crore from ₹16,600 crore in March 2026. The management noted that cement prices adjust with a lag to structural changes in costs. Prices are therefore expected to rise further in the near term as companies seek to offset higher expenses. Domestic cement demand is estimated to have grown 10 per cent Y-o-Y in Q2FY27, while UltraTech reported volume growth of 13.8 per cent, indicating market share gains. Capacity utilisation increased to 71 per cent in Q2FY27 from 66 per cent in Q2FY26.
 Demand is expected to pick up from mid-November, after the festival season. Urban housing, infrastructure and private-sector capex are likely to remain key growth drivers. The net debt-to-Ebitda ratio is expected to remain broadly stable at 0.8-1.0 times. Return on equity (RoE) and return on capital employed (RoCE) are projected to rise by 100 bps each in FY28 compared with FY26, as more scale creates better operating leverage.
 In the C&W business, the focus is on scaling up production. With an annualised copper consumption capacity of 78,000 tonnes, UltraVolt ranks second in terms of installed capacity and is not expected to require additional investment beyond the planned capex to maintain its position. The company has introduced differentiated products rather than competing primarily on price. The business is expected to mature in FY28. Given the encouraging feedback from the launch, it may scale up faster.
 UltraTech has extended its lead in cement capacity and market share while maintaining its cost leadership and strong cash flow generation. Most analysts are retaining or marginally raising their earnings per share (EPS) estimates for FY27 and FY28, factoring in low-to-mid-teens growth in revenue and Ebitda.
 The stock is valued at around 17 times its estimated FY27 enterprise value (EV)-to-Ebitda. While some analysts may upgrade their valuations, others are maintaining them. Key risks include rising costs and flatter demand because pricing power is moderate.

docs.title: 3 ‘Buy’ recommendations by Jefferies with 22% to 41% upside
docs.text: A stock falling sharply, rising costs or an expensive business expansion can make investors question whether an opportunity is emerging or more downside lies ahead. Global investment bank Jefferies has identified three stocks where it sees potential upside, although each faces a different challenge. Jefferies has retained its ‘Buy’ rating on Crompton Greaves Consumer Electricals, Mankind Pharma and IndiGo, with target prices indicating potential gains of 41%, 37% and 22%, respectively. According to the report, these opportunities come with risks ranging from commodity inflation and uncertain drug development to elevated aviation fuel costs. Let's take a look at why Jefferies is bullish on this stock and the rationale behind it - Jefferies on Crompton Greaves: Can festive demand offset rising costs? Jefferies has set a target price of Rs 305 for Crompton Greaves Consumer Electricals. This translates to an upside of 41% from the current market price. The global investment bank has retained its 'Buy' rating to the stock despite concerns about input costs and pressure on margins. As per the report, Crompton's Q2FY27 profit after tax was in line with expectations. Furthermore, the sales grew 18% year-on-year. Also, adjusted profit after tax rose 30%. ALSO READ‘Data centre in a container’: The multibillion-dollar opportunity and 2 stocks to watch In addition to this, the company has also increased prices in its electrical consumer durables segment to manage higher input costs. However, inflation continues to affect its lighting and Butterfly businesses. Jefferies noted that "input cost pressure continues, impacting YoY margins in Lighting, Butterfly." It also cautioned that "inflationary pressures warrant caution - both for demand and margins." The brokerage believes the stock's valuation offers a favourable risk-reward balance after its 17% fall over six months. Festive-season demand, commodity prices and the company's ability to protect margins will remain important factors to watch. Jefferies on Mankind Pharma: A cancer-treatment bet with a long road ahead Jefferies has assigned Mankind Pharma a target price of Rs 3,220, implying an upside of 37%. Its analysis focuses on the company's decision to acquire a 70% stake in Belgium-based Armed Cell Therapeutics (ACTx) for 48 million euros. The acquisition gives Mankind access to next-generation chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapies, which are designed to help the immune system recognise and attack cancer cells. The company's lead programmes target non-Hodgkin lymphoma and small-cell lung cancer. However, these treatments are still at an early development stage. That means it could take considerable time before they generate revenue, while research and development may require additional investment. Jefferies described the acquisition as part of Mankind's strategy to build a global, innovation-led pharmaceutical business. The report warned that "its early-stage nature is likely to lead to a long gestation period and may require cash outflows to fund development." Jefferies on IndiGo: Will lower costs and higher fares restore earnings? In the aviation sector, Jefferies has set a target price of Rs 5,840 for IndiGo. This indicates an upside of 22% from the current market price. The airline's shares have fallen 25% from their August 2026 highs, as per the report. ALSO READAxis Bank vs ICICI Bank: Jefferies sees up to 32% upside in one stock – Here’s why The prolonged conflict in West Asia has kept aviation fuel costs elevated. Airlines have responded by increasing fares and managing capacity, but higher ticket prices can also affect passenger demand. IndiGo received 10 Airbus aircraft in September 2026, taking its deliveries for the calendar year to 39. However, adding aircraft without sufficient utilisation can increase costs per passenger. Jefferies said "sustained earnings recovery is contingent only on conflict resolution, given continued fuel cost pressures." The winter flying schedule could support capacity growth in the second half of FY27. However, fuel prices, aircraft utilisation and passenger demand will determine whether that translates into stronger earnings. What investors need to watch Jefferies sees potential upside in Crompton Greaves, Mankind Pharma and IndiGo, but their recovery depends on different factors. While Crompton needs to manage rising costs, Mankind’s acquisition will take time to deliver results, and IndiGo’s earnings recovery hinges on fuel costs and demand. docs.title: Axis Bank vs ICICI Bank: Jefferies sees up to 32% upside in one stock – Here’s why
docs.text: Two of India’s big private sector lenders reported results for the July-September 2026 quarter. Global investment bank Jefferies has kept its 'Buy' rating on both Axis Bank and ICICI Bank but they see different upside potential for the stocks. The price tag investors should watch Jefferies has set a target of Rs 1,700 for Axis Bank, which implies a rise of about 32%. For ICICI Bank, the target is Rs 1,750, with a rise of roughly 25% shown in the report. The numbers behind the calls came in better than the global investment bank had forecast. Axis Bank’s profit rose 38% from a year earlier to Rs 7,000 crore, while ICICI Bank’s grew 20% to Rs 14,800 crore. Both lenders did well on earnings and on bad loans, but Jefferies sees different strengths and different gaps in each. Jefferies on Axis Bank: Can better margins lift profitability? Axis Bank reported a 38% year-on-year increase in standalone net profit to Rs 7,000 crore for the September quarter, beating Jefferies’ estimates. ALSO READWhy UltraTech Cement is near its 52-week low despite 25.2% profit growth According to the Jefferies report, higher income and lower provisions supported the performance, while net interest income (NII) grew 12% year-on-year. Jefferies noted that core net interest margin (NIM), which measures the profitability of a bank’s lending and deposit activities, remained stable sequentially. However, the impact of foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR-B) deposits was higher than expected. Jefferies said, “NII growth ahead of estimates aided by better margins.” It expects Axis Bank to gradually shift its lending towards retail customers and small and medium enterprises, which could help improve margins and return on equity (ROE). Jefferies also highlighted improving asset quality. Axis Bank’s gross non-performing loan (NPL) ratio stood at 1.2%, while its specific coverage ratio was 70%. Jefferies has retained its 'Buy' rating and Rs 1,700 target price, citing attractive valuations of 10 times estimated price-to-earnings (P/E) and 1.3 times adjusted price-to-book value for FY28. Jefferies on ICICI Bank: Stronger income growth, but margins need watching ICICI Bank reported a 20% year-on-year rise in standalone net profit to Rs 14,800 crore for the September quarter, ahead of Jefferies’ estimates. Its net interest income increased 18% year-on-year, outpacing Axis Bank’s 12% growth. However, ICICI Bank’s core net interest margin declined by 10 basis points sequentially to 4.2%. According to Jefferies, the higher share of corporate loans and the impact of FCNR-B deposits weighed on margins. The global investment bank expects a normalisation in the bank’s asset mix and the repricing of loans following interest rate increases to support margins in the coming quarters. It said, “Stronger NII growth; normalisation of asset mix will aid margins.” ICICI Bank’s gross and net NPL ratios stood at 1.2% and 0.3%, respectively. Jefferies noted that lower credit costs supported quarterly earnings and expects the bank to deliver 16% compound annual growth in core profit between FY26-29. ALSO READCEAT share price: Nomura sees 22% upside on EV bet despite delay in margin recovery Jefferies has maintained its Buy rating and raised its earnings estimates by 5-6%. It has set a target price of Rs 1,750, based on a sum-of-the-parts valuation, which values the bank using different business segments. Axis Bank vs ICICI Bank: What should investors watch? The key difference lies in valuations and earnings drivers. Jefferies sees Axis Bank benefiting from a shift towards higher-yielding loans and improved profitability, while ICICI Bank’s stronger income growth and expected loan repricing could support future earnings. docs.title: Mukul Agrawal’s latest moves: A Rs 189 cr mining bet and 4 newly listed SME stocks
docs.text: Mukul Agrawal Portfolio 2026: A ₹261 Crore Bet on New SME Stocks Mukul Agrawal does not buy quietly. The shareholding filings for the quarter ending September 2026 show 5 new names in the Param Capital founder's book, per public records. The portfolio is now worth over Rs 8,000 cr across 76 stocks. Together, those five stakes are worth about Rs 261 cr. Nearly 72% of that sits in just one company, Tega Industries. The rest is spread across four small and medium enterprise (SME) stocks that listed only this year. Here is what each company does, what the numbers say, and what could go wrong. #1 Tega Industries: Inside Agrawal's ₹189 Crore Mining Investment Incorporated in 1976, Tega Industries makes the wear parts that keep mines running. Mill liners, screens and other consumables used to crush, grind and move ore. Because these consumables inevitably wear out, customers generate recurring revenue. It was the second-largest maker of polymer-based mill liners by 2020 revenue. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now In June 2026, Tega closed its purchase of Molycop, a global maker of grinding media, in a roughly $1.5 billion deal done with funds managed by Apollo. Mukul Agrawal paid for a piece of that deal. Filings on BSE and NSE show he was allotted 5,01,504 shares at Rs 1,994 each on 28th November 2025, as part of Tega's Rs 1,713 cr preferential issue. That was about Rs 100 cr, or 0.67% of the company, below the 1% line where investors get named. By September 2026, he had crossed it. His stake now stands at 1.33%, which works out to roughly 10 lakh shares, about double his original allotment, a holding worth close to Rs 190 cr. Sales jumped to Rs 1,723 cr, of which Molycop contributed about Rs 1,292 cr for just one month. Yet Tega posted a net loss of Rs 108 cr. Per the company's filing, about Rs 191 cr of one-time deal costs hit that quarter. Excluding them, adjusted profit was about Rs 55 cr, up 26%. Tega Industries Debt Risk: Navigating a 99x PE Ratio in 2026 The share price of Tega Industries was Rs 453 at its IPO in December 2021. As of closing on 16th October 2026, it was Rs 1,923, a gain of about 324%. That is still about 5% below the Rs 1,994 Mukul paid in the preferential issue. Screener shows the PE to be in the negative, but on FY26 earnings, the stock is priced at about 99x, against a current industry median of 35x. The June loss makes the trailing PE meaningless, and with under five years of listed history, there is no 10-year median to compare. The real risk is debt. Before the deal, borrowings stood at Rs 398 cr in March 2026. Interest alone came to Rs 117 cr in the June quarter, against Rs 24 cr for all of FY26. Management calls cutting debt its first job. Some governance rules for larger firms do not apply. Volumes are thin, so prices swing hard on small orders. And supply can jump when lock-ins end. #2 Anawil Wire and Engineering: Why Mukul Agrawal and Sunil Singhania Are Buying Incorporated in January 2021, Anawil Wire and Engineering makes the steel towers that hold up wind turbines, up to 140 metres tall. docs.title: 57x growth in solar capacity: 2 stocks betting big on India’s next solar wave
docs.text: India’s solar energy sector is entering a new phase of growth. Installed solar capacity has increased from less than 3 gigawatts (GW) in 2014 to around 171 GW in 2026, driven by rising electricity demand amid a shift towards renewable energy. The pace of expansion is also picking up. India added around 34 GW of solar capacity in the first half of 2026, up 38% year-on-year, while full-year additions are projected to reach nearly 50 GW. This growth brings opportunities across the solar value chain. Domestic manufacturing is expanding as companies invest in solar modules, cells, and upstream production facilities. At the same time, the rising number of utility-scale solar projects is creating demand for engineering, procurement, construction, and renewable energy asset management services. Upstream Integration vs. Turnkey EPC: Structural Comparison Against this backdrop, this article looks at two distinct business models that offer an interesting perspective on India’s solar growth story. One is strengthening its position through domestic solar manufacturing, capacity expansion, and backward integration, while the other is building its business around renewable energy project execution and a growing international footprint. It is a pure-play solar PV manufacturer specializing in TOPCon (Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact) cell and solar module production. It has a research partnership with Fraunhofer ISE (Europe’s leading solar research institute) to optimize TOPCon efficiency. Scaling Up: Solar Module and TOPCon Cell Roadmap to 2028 The installed capacity of solar modules is 10.3 GW and that of solar TOPCon cells is 2.9 GW. Its cell plant achieved an 89% effective utilization rate in Q2FY27. It is adding 6 GW of solar module capacity by December 2026 and 6 GW of TOPCon cell capacity by March 2027. This expansion will increase total annual capacity to 16.3 GW for modules and 8.9 GW for cells by early FY28. Backward Integration: The ₹5,500-Crore Ingot & Wafer Bet Further, the company plans to build a 9 GW ingot and wafer manufacturing facility. The capacity will be rolled out in two phases, with 5 GW in FY29 and 4 GW in FY30. This move is designed to secure raw material supplies internally. The estimated capital expenditure of ₹5,000-5,500 crore for this capacity will be funded mainly through internal cash flows. Regulatory Tailwinds: ALMM List II and Domestic Cell Premiums The company boasts an order book of 10.4 GW as of September 30, 2026, with 1.5 GW of new order inflows in Q2FY27. In addition, complex tenders for hybrid and round-the-clock power require up to 2x DC module capacity relative to AC grid connections. The Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List II also became active on June 1, 2026. Regulatory Push: Why ALMM List II Unlocks 40 GW of Protected Demand Current projects under net-metering and open-access have a transition period until December 31, 2026, after which full List II compliance is required. Solar modules built using domestic cells command a price premium of roughly 60% higher than modules assembled with imported cells. Programs like PM Surya Ghar, PM-KUSUM create a domestic demand pool of at least 40 GW for Indian cell and module makers. Emmvee has aligned its manufacturing expansion, product listings, and supply chain strategy to capture this regulatory shift. Emmvee’s G12R TOPCon solar cells are officially included under the ALMM List. This qualification allows it to supply domestic cells directly to government schemes and commercial projects requiring DCR compliance. Financial Trajectory: 35.3% Margins and Cash Flow Acceleration On the financial front, the company’s revenue rose 39% year-on-year to ₹1,576.4 crore in Q2FY27. EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortisation) also surged 39% to ₹556.9 crore as margins steadied at 35.3% in Q2FY27. Consequently, net profit increased by 61% to ₹382 crore aided by interest savings (₹45.7 crore). Emmvee management expects to reach the upper end of its FY27 EBITDA target of ₹2,200 crore to ₹2,400 crore. Of this, it has already reached ₹1,105 crore in H1FY27. Management expects to deliver 5.0 to 5.5 GW of the order backlog within the next 12 to 15 months. Operating cash flow after working capital changes grew to ₹409.9 crore in H1FY27, up from ₹131.0 crore in H1FY26. In 2022, Reliance New Energy (part of the Reliance Group) acquired a 40% stake in the company. docs.title: ‘We are positive on duration bonds’: Basant Bafna
docs.text: With the RBI raising the repo rate by 25 basis points, Basant Bafna, head of fixed income at Mirae Asset Mutual Fund, expects another 50 bps of rate hikes in FY27. In an interview with Christina Titus, he says the benchmark 10-year bond yield is likely to remain around current levels, making this a favourable time for investors to lock in longer durations. Excerpts: How do you expect interest rates to move going forward? We expect another 50 basis points of rate hikes in FY27, implemented in a calibrated manner, with an additional 25 bps depending on evolving macroeconomic and geopolitical conditions. However, markets are currently pricing in a significantly sharper increase of 100 bps, amid persistent global uncertainties and the RBI's continued measures to stabilise the rupee. ALSO READ3 ‘Buy’ recommendations by Jefferies with 22% to 41% upside Given that interest rate differentials have narrowed significantly, partly due to robust domestic fundamentals, our base case is that a modest rate hike at this stage is unlikely to attract substantial inflows. The scale of rate hikes required to draw foreign investment into debt markets would be significantly larger. How do you see liquidity conditions evolving? Monday's variable rate repo (VRR) operation shows that the RBI remains nimble in managing liquidity on both sides. Recent forex measures have also affected liquidity. Although liquidity has declined, I do not expect the RBI to immediately reverse its measures to stabilise the rupee, as these were intended to curb speculative activity. Against the backdrop of tightening liquidity, we expect the RBI to provide intermittent support through VRR operations rather than durable liquidity infusion, given its calibrated tightening stance. Government cash balances also remain high, and liquidity should improve as government spending picks up and funds flow into the economy. At what levels do you expect the benchmark 10-year bond yield to trade in the near term? We believe the longer end of the yield curve has already priced in most of the negatives, including expected policy rate movements and spreads. The curve has begun showing signs of flattening. While the longer end remains relatively stable, the shorter end continues to witness volatility amid evolving geopolitical conditions. Historically, the median spread between the 10-year government security yield and the repo rate has been 105–110 bps. At 7.35–7.40%, the 10-year yield already factors in a repo rate of 6.25%. Therefore, we do not expect a significant sell-off, and yields should remain around current levels in the near term. How has your portfolio strategy evolved with the shift towards a rate-hike cycle? We are increasing allocations to sovereign bonds in the 14-year, 30-year and 40-year maturity segments. In corporate bonds, we favour the five-year and 10-year segments. We have also begun tactically adding duration in a calibrated manner. While the shorter end of the yield curve continues to offer value, the curve could flatten further if geopolitical tensions remain elevated for a prolonged period. Which part of the yield curve offers the most attractive investment opportunities? It depends on the investment horizon. For investors with a three-to-six-month horizon, ultra-short-duration or money-market funds are appropriate. Those with a six-to-12-month horizon can consider ultra-short- to short-duration funds. For investors looking to lock in longer durations, this is a very good time. Those nearing retirement could consider long-tenor bonds alongside a systematic withdrawal plan to support their long-term financial needs. Given the relative stability at the longer end of the yield curve, investors with an appropriate risk appetite should consider increasing duration. How do you view India's growth and inflation outlook? Growth remains robust, with the upcoming festive season expected to provide further support. However, the lagged effects of El Niño and depleted groundwater levels could affect the rabi crop, posing risks to inflation. At the same time, a significant portion of price pressures has yet to be passed on to consumers. With wholesale price inflation running well above consumer inflation, the GDP deflator is expected to remain elevated, pushing nominal GDP growth into double digits. The rabi season and persistently high crude oil prices will need close monitoring, as both could pose upside risks to inflation. We expect inflation at 5.2–5.3% and economic growth of around 7% in FY27. What further steps can India take to attract FPI inflows into its debt markets, beyond the tax cuts and other measures already introduced? The key is to engage closely with passive index providers, address ease-of-doing-business concerns and ensure policy continuity. Meeting their requirements will help sustain structural passive inflows into the economy. ALSO READIndian IT stocks rally 12% in a week – Is the turnaround sustainable? In the near term, narrow yield spreads will continue to weigh on foreign investment. However, as India gains wider acceptance as a structural allocation destination, passive flows should build steadily. Tactical inflows could also pick up once concerns over crude oil prices subside. What is your assessment of India's move towards tokenisation of corporate bonds? It is a step in the right direction, but adoption by issuers and investors will take time, given the multiple issuances within each maturity bucket. We are closely monitoring developments and will consider participating once we see meaningful improvements in market liquidity.

docs.title: Jio’s Rs 30,213 cr IPO: What the mega Rs 10.3 lakh cr valuation means for RIL
docs.text: For Reliance Industries shareholders, the upcoming listing of Jio Platforms raises a question that goes beyond telecom tariffs, 5G services and digital subscriptions. This is - Will putting a separate market price on Jio unlock more value for the parent company, or has the stock market already accounted for it? Jio Platforms, the digital and telecom arm of Mukesh Ambani-led Reliance Industries, is set to launch its Rs 30,213 crore initial public offering (IPO) on October 21. At the upper end of the price band, the company will be valued at around Rs 10.3 lakh crore. Reliance Industries (RIL), which owns 66.43% of Jio, holds a stake worth approximately Rs 6.8 lakh crore at this valuation. However, the value of Jio's shares and the value investors assign to RIL are not necessarily the same. The difference could determine how much of the listing's potential benefit reaches RIL shareholders. Why Jio's listing matters for RIL Until now, investors have had to assess Jio's contribution as part of Reliance Industries' wider business. A separate listing will give the telecom and digital services business its own market price, making it easier to estimate its value independently. ALSO READJio IPO GMP surges 22% ahead of launch: 4 big risks every investor must watch first This could help investors assess RIL's different businesses more clearly. Apart from Jio, the conglomerate has interests in retail, oil-to-chemicals (O2C) and new energy, each with its own growth prospects, risks and investment requirements. Religare Broking believes the listing could change how investors value the parent company. In its report, the brokerage said the IPO could be a "structural inflection point for group re-rating", as it would provide greater transparency into the value of RIL's investments. The brokerage added that listing Jio would provide an independent market price for the group's largest growth asset, helping investors evaluate Reliance's sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) valuation. This method estimates a company's worth by valuing its individual businesses separately and then combining those values. Religare also argued that investors often price in major corporate events before they happen. Buying RIL only after Jio's listing could therefore mean missing part of any potential valuation change. The holding company discount: Why the numbers may not add up A company that owns many businesses often trades for less than the combined value of those businesses. This gap is called the holding company discount. Investors may feel the parent is complicated, that taxes could eat into any sale of assets, or that nobody knows when the value will actually reach them. RIL is a good example. It spans oil refining, chemicals, telecom, retail and new energy, and the market must price all of it in one share. A listed Jio changes the game because there will be a daily market price for its biggest growth business. ALSO READThe Rs 10 Lakh Cr digital giant: Is Jio Platforms’ 34x P/E band built for a rerating? For RIL, the key question is whether its current share price already reflects a lower valuation for its Jio stake. Motilal Oswal, in a report dated October 6, 2026, estimates Jio Platforms' equity value at around Rs 11 lakh crore, close to its own valuation of Rs 11.2 lakh crore. At that level, Jio would trade at approximately 12 times its estimated FY28 enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EV/EBITDA). Despite the potential for greater transparency after listing, Motilal Oswal believes much of the holding company discount may already be reflected in RIL's valuation. Its estimates suggest that the market is applying an 18-36% discount to RIL's Jio stake, depending on the valuation multiple assigned to Reliance Retail Ventures. What investors should watch next The IPO consists entirely of a fresh issue of 27 crore shares, with a price band of Rs 1,065-1,119 per share. At the upper end, the issue size is Rs 30,213 crore. Following the issue, RIL's ownership will decline from 66.43% to 64.48%. The key test will be how the market values Jio once it begins trading independently and whether that valuation changes investors' assessment of Reliance Industries.
